investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What do the letters in CURB-65 stand for?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Confusion (new; AMTS ≤8 or new disorientation), Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate ≥30/min, Blood pressure (SBP <90 or DBP ≤60), age ≥65. One point each, maximum 5.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How does CRB-65 differ from CURB-65, and why?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: CRB-65 omits the Urea component so it can be used in primary care/community settings where blood tests are not available. Maximum score is 4 instead of 5.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Give the CURB-65 bands with approximate mortality and disposition.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 0–1 = low severity, mortality <3%, consider home/oral antibiotics. 2 = moderate, mortality ~9%, consider hospital/short-stay. 3–5 = high severity, mortality 15–40%, admit and assess for ICU/HDU.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How does CURB-65 severity guide empirical antibiotic choice (NICE/BTS)?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Low severity: oral amoxicillin (macrolide/doxycycline if penicillin-allergic). High severity: dual therapy with co-amoxiclav + a macrolide, often IV, with critical-care review.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Why must CURB-65 not be used in isolation?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: It is an adjunct to clinical judgement. It underweights young patients and comorbidity — a young person can be critically ill with a low score. Always assess SaO₂/oxygen need, comorbidity, radiographic extent, and social factors.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: State the three Light's criteria for an exudate.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: ANY ONE of: (1) pleural protein / serum protein > 0.5; (2) pleural LDH / serum LDH > 0.6; (3) pleural LDH > 0.66 (two-thirds) the upper limit of normal serum LDH. If none are met, it is a transudate.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What paired samples must you send to apply Light's criteria?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Simultaneous pleural fluid AND serum for total protein and LDH.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Give the typical causes of a transudative vs an exudative pleural effusion.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Transudate (pressure-driven): heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia, hypothyroidism, Meigs. Exudate (permeability/local disease): infection (parapneumonic/empyema/TB), malignancy, PE, pancreatitis, RA/SLE.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: A patient on diuretics for heart failure has fluid labelled exudate by Light's criteria, but you suspect a transudate. What do you do?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Light's over-identifies exudates in diuretic-treated patients. Calculate the serum-minus-pleural albumin gradient: > 12 g/L supports a transudate.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Pleural fluid pH is 7.1 in a patient with pneumonia. What does this mean and what is the action?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: pH < 7.2 indicates a complicated parapneumonic effusion (or empyema if pus/organisms). It requires a chest drain, not antibiotics alone.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the four Centor criteria (1 point each)?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Tonsillar exudate; tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy; history of fever >38C; absence of cough. (Higher score = higher probability of group A strep.)

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How does the Modified (McIsaac) Centor score adjust for age?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: +1 point if 3-14 years, 0 if 15-44 years, and -1 if 45 years or older.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What do the letters of FeverPAIN stand for (1 point each, max 5)?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Fever in last 24h; Purulence; Attend rapidly (within 3 days of onset); severely Inflamed tonsils; No cough or coryza.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What is the NICE antibiotic decision by FeverPAIN band?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 0-1 (or Centor 0-2): no antibiotic. 2-3: consider delayed/back-up antibiotic. 4-5 (or Centor 3-4): consider immediate antibiotic (phenoxymethylpenicillin; clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Why must amoxicillin be avoided in undifferentiated tonsillitis?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: If the cause is glandular fever (EBV/infectious mononucleosis), amoxicillin causes a widespread maculopapular rash. Phenoxymethylpenicillin is preferred when an antibiotic is indicated.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What is the two-level Wells (PE) score and its decision threshold?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Weighted points: DVT signs 3, PE #1 diagnosis 3, HR>100 1.5, immobilisation/surgery <4wk 1.5, previous VTE 1.5, haemoptysis 1, malignancy 1. ≤4 = PE unlikely (do a D-dimer); >4 = PE likely (CTPA directly).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: A patient is Wells "PE likely" (>4). What is the next step, and what if CTPA is delayed or contraindicated?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Arrange CTPA directly — a D-dimer is not indicated (poor specificity cannot exclude PE at high probability). If CTPA is delayed, give interim anticoagulation; if contraindicated (renal impairment, contrast allergy, pregnancy) use a V/Q scan.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: When can PERC be used, and what does an all-negative result allow?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: PERC applies only when clinical gestalt is already low-probability. If all 8 criteria are negative (age<50, HR<100, SaO₂≥95%, no haemoptysis, no oestrogen, no prior VTE, no unilateral leg swelling, no recent surgery/trauma), PE risk is <2% — rule out with no D-dimer and no imaging.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: List the life-threatening features of acute asthma.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: PEF <33%, SpO₂ <92% (PaO₂ <8 kPa), silent chest, cyanosis or poor effort, exhaustion/altered consciousness, arrhythmia/hypotension, and a normal PaCO₂ (4.6–6.0). Any one (in an acute-severe attack) = life-threatening.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What defines acute severe asthma (any one feature)?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: PEF 33–50% best/predicted, RR ≥25, HR ≥110, or inability to complete sentences in one breath. Moderate asthma is PEF 50–75% with none of these.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How does acute asthma management escalate with severity?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: O₂ to SpO₂ 94–98%; salbutamol nebs (back-to-back if severe); add ipratropium in severe/life-threatening; early steroids (oral prednisolone or IV hydrocortisone); IV magnesium sulfate if poor response; ITU/anaesthetic referral for life-threatening or near-fatal.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the five DECAF components (acute COPD exacerbation)?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Dyspnoea (eMRCD 5a=1, 5b=2), Eosinopenia (<0.05), Consolidation on CXR, Acidaemia (pH<7.30), atrial Fibrillation. Score 0–6, predicting in-hospital mortality.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does a low vs high DECAF score mean for management?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 0–1: low mortality — consider supported/early discharge. 2: intermediate — admit. 3–6: high mortality — escalate, senior review, discuss ceiling of care / ITU & NIV. Respiratory acidosis (pH<7.35) → NIV.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What do the letters of STOP-BANG stand for?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Snoring, Tiredness, Observed apnoea, Pressure (treated HTN), BMI>35, Age>50, Neck>40cm, Gender male. One point each (max 8).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What action does a STOP-BANG score drive?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: ≥3 → refer for a sleep study (home oximetry/polysomnography) to confirm and grade OSA. Confirmed moderate–severe OSA → CPAP, weight loss, avoid alcohol/sedatives, and DVLA advice if sleepy. STOP-BANG screens; it does not diagnose.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Which chest-pain risk score is used in the ED for undifferentiated chest pain, and what does it predict?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: The HEART score. It risk-stratifies undifferentiated chest pain for 6-week major adverse cardiac events (MACE) and guides safe discharge versus admission.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: List the five HEART score components and their point range.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, Troponin — each scored 0, 1 or 2, for a total of 0–10. Bands: 0–3 low, 4–6 moderate, 7–10 high.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the seven TIMI (UA/NSTEMI) variables and what does the score predict?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Age ≥65; ≥3 CAD risk factors; known CAD (≥50% stenosis); aspirin use in last 7 days; ≥2 anginal episodes in 24h; ST deviation ≥0.5mm; raised cardiac markers. Each 1 point (0–7); predicts 14-day risk of death, MI or urgent revascularisation.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Which variables make up the GRACE score and what does it predict?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Age, heart rate, systolic BP, creatinine, Killip class, cardiac arrest at admission, ST-segment deviation, and elevated cardiac enzymes. It predicts in-hospital and 6-month mortality after ACS.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How does the GRACE score guide management in the UK (NICE)?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: GRACE estimates mortality risk after NSTEMI/UA; a 6-month mortality >3% (intermediate-to-high risk) means the patient should be offered early invasive coronary angiography, typically within 72 hours.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does CHA₂DS₂-VASc estimate and in whom?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Annual risk of ischaemic stroke / systemic thromboembolism in non-valvular AF, used to decide whether to start anticoagulation (DOAC first-line).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Which CHA₂DS₂-VASc components score 2 points?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Age ≥75 (A₂) and prior Stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (S₂). Maximum total score is 9.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: At what CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is anticoagulation offered?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Offer anticoagulation if ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women. Consider it if 1 in men. Score 0 (men) or 1 in a woman from the sex point alone = no anticoagulation.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What is the purpose of HAS-BLED and what does a score ≥3 mean?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: It estimates 1-year major bleeding risk to flag modifiable risk factors. A score ≥3 = high risk: review and correct modifiable factors — it is NOT a reason to withhold anticoagulation.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: List the HAS-BLED components.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Hypertension (uncontrolled SBP >160), Abnormal renal/liver function (1 each), Stroke, Bleeding history/predisposition, Labile INR, Elderly >65, Drugs (antiplatelets/NSAIDs)/alcohol (1 each).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the two MAJOR criteria in the Modified Duke Criteria?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: (1) Positive blood cultures with a typical IE organism from 2 separate cultures (or persistently positive, or single Coxiella burnetii/phase I IgG >1:800). (2) Evidence of endocardial involvement on echo (vegetation, abscess, new prosthetic dehiscence) or new valvular regurgitation.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: List the five MINOR Duke criteria.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 1) Predisposition (predisposing heart condition or IVDU); 2) Fever ≥38°C; 3) Vascular phenomena (septic emboli, Janeway lesions, mycotic aneurysm, conjunctival haemorrhage); 4) Immunologic phenomena (Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis, rheumatoid factor); 5) Microbiological evidence not meeting a major criterion.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What combinations give a diagnosis of DEFINITE infective endocarditis?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 2 major criteria, OR 1 major + 3 minor, OR 5 minor criteria.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What combinations give a diagnosis of POSSIBLE infective endocarditis?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 1 major + 1 minor, OR 3 minor criteria.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How do Janeway lesions differ from Osler nodes, and which criterion does each fall under?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Janeway lesions are painless and are a vascular phenomenon; Osler nodes are painful ('Ouch') and are an immunologic phenomenon.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the two highest-weighted components of the Wells score for PE, and how many points each?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Clinical signs of DVT (3 points) and "PE is the #1 diagnosis or equally likely" (3 points). All other components score 1.5 (HR>100, immobilisation/surgery in 4 weeks, previous DVT/PE) or 1 (haemoptysis, malignancy).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Using the two-level Wells score, what test follows a score of ≤4 versus >4?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: ≤4 = PE unlikely → D-dimer (CTPA only if positive). >4 = PE likely → go straight to CTPA (D-dimer not needed); give interim anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What is PERC and when is it applied?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: The PE Rule-out Criteria: 8 criteria (age<50, HR<100, SaO₂≥95%, no haemoptysis, no oestrogen, no prior DVT/PE, no unilateral leg swelling, no recent surgery/trauma). Used ONLY in low pre-test probability — if all 8 are negative, PE is ruled out with no D-dimer and no imaging.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does sPESI predict and what do the scores mean?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Simplified PESI is prognostic (not diagnostic): it predicts 30-day mortality in CONFIRMED PE. Variables (1 pt each): age>80, cancer, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, HR≥110, SBP<100, SaO₂<90%. Score 0 = low risk (~1% mortality) → consider outpatient management; ≥1 = admit.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How and why is D-dimer age-adjusted, and when should D-dimer be avoided?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: In patients over 50, use age×10 µg/L as the cut-off (e.g. 750 at age 75) to improve poor specificity and reduce unnecessary CTPAs. Avoid D-dimer in high-probability (Wells>4) patients — a normal result does not exclude PE; go directly to CTPA.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the two Wells DVT categories and their cut-offs (NICE two-level model)?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Score ≥2 = DVT likely; score ≤1 = DVT unlikely.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Which single Wells DVT item scores negative points, and how many?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: −2 if an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely as DVT. All other items score +1.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: A patient is 'DVT likely' (Wells ≥2). What does NICE recommend?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Proximal leg vein ultrasound within 4 hours. If not available within 4h, give interim anticoagulation and do a D-dimer, with the scan within 24 hours.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: A patient is 'DVT unlikely' (Wells ≤1). What is the next step?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: D-dimer. If positive, proceed to proximal leg vein ultrasound. If negative, DVT is excluded and an alternative diagnosis is sought.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Ultrasound is negative but D-dimer is positive and Wells is 'likely'. What now?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Repeat the proximal ultrasound scan in 6–8 days, because an isolated distal (calf) DVT may have been missed and can propagate.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What must every patient admitted to a UK hospital receive, and why?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: A documented VTE risk assessment (NICE) — a nationally mandated safety metric. It balances thrombosis risk against bleeding risk to decide on mechanical and/or pharmacological prophylaxis, because VTE is a leading cause of preventable hospital death.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: List key NICE VTE (thrombosis) risk factors.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Active cancer, age >60, dehydration, known thrombophilia, obesity (BMI >30), ≥1 significant comorbidity, personal/first-degree family history of VTE, HRT/oestrogen contraceptive, varicose veins with phlebitis, reduced mobility ≥3 days, and surgery (especially >90 min or lower limb/pelvis).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Name NICE bleeding risk factors that count against pharmacological prophylaxis.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Active bleeding; acquired/inherited bleeding disorder (e.g. haemophilia); concurrent therapeutic anticoagulation; acute stroke; uncontrolled hypertension (>230/120); LP/epidural/spinal within 4h (or expected within 12h); thrombocytopenia (platelets <75).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How does the Caprini score stratify surgical VTE risk?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: A points-based model (factors weighted 1–5). 0 = very low (ambulation); 1–2 = low (mechanical/IPC); 3–4 = moderate (pharmacological ± mechanical); ≥5 = high (pharmacological + mechanical, consider extended LMWH).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: First-line prophylaxis agents and durations under NICE?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: LMWH is first-line pharmacological prophylaxis; fondaparinux if LMWH unsuitable (e.g. HIT); UFH in severe renal impairment. Continue until mobile/discharge, but extend for elective hip replacement (up to 35 days), knee replacement (10–14 days), and abdominal/pelvic cancer surgery (28 days).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What is QRISK3 and who is it for?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: A UK primary-prevention calculator estimating a person’s 10-year risk of a first MI or stroke, for adults 25–84 without established CVD. It combines age, sex, ethnicity, deprivation, smoking, diabetes, BP, cholesterol/HDL ratio, BMI and conditions such as CKD, AF, RA and SLE.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What QRISK3 threshold triggers a statin, and which one?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: A 10-year CVD risk of ≥10% → offer atorvastatin 20 mg for primary prevention (after lifestyle advice). Below 10% → lifestyle measures and periodic reassessment.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Name the groups who are statin-eligible without calculating QRISK3.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Established CVD (MI, stroke/TIA, PAD, angina) → secondary prevention with atorvastatin 80 mg. Type 1 diabetes, CKD, and familial hypercholesterolaemia → statin-eligible regardless (QRISK3 under-estimates their risk).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Describe the four NYHA classes of heart failure.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: I: no limitation. II: slight limitation — symptoms on ordinary activity. III: marked limitation — symptoms on less-than-ordinary activity. IV: symptoms at rest.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How does NYHA class guide heart-failure management?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Symptomatic HFrEF (NYHA II–IV, reduced EF) → start/up-titrate the four pillars (ACEi/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i). Persistent NYHA II–IV with LVEF ≤35% despite optimal therapy → refer for CRT/ICD.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What defines Ann Arbor Stage II lymphoma?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Involvement of two or more lymph node regions on the SAME side of the diaphragm. (Stage I = single region/single extralymphatic site; Stage III = both sides of diaphragm; Stage IV = disseminated extralymphatic involvement e.g. marrow, liver, lung.)

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the B symptoms and what suffix do they give?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, and unintentional weight loss >10% of body weight over 6 months. Their presence gives the suffix B (absence = A); B carries a worse prognosis.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What do the Ann Arbor suffixes E and S mean?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: E = localised contiguous extranodal (extralymphatic) extension from a nodal site; S = splenic involvement.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: List the 5 IPI factors for aggressive NHL (mnemonic APLES).
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Age >60; Performance status ECOG ≥2; LDH raised (above normal); Extranodal sites >1; Stage (Ann Arbor) III or IV. One point each, total 0–5.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How do IPI scores map to risk groups, and what does R-IPI/FLIPI refer to?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 0–1 low, 2 low-intermediate, 3 high-intermediate, 4–5 high risk (predicting overall survival). R-IPI is the revised index for R-CHOP-treated DLBCL; FLIPI is the separate prognostic index for follicular lymphoma.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does the CRAB acronym stand for in multiple myeloma?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: hyperCalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone lesions — the four classic end-organ damage features that define symptomatic myeloma requiring treatment.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the CRAB threshold values?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: C: corrected Ca >2.75 mmol/L (or >0.25 above ULN). R: creatinine >177 µmol/L or eGFR <40. A: Hb <100 g/L (or >20 below normal). B: ≥1 osteolytic lesion (≥5 mm) — osteoporosis or a compression fracture alone does not count.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the SLiM biomarkers added by the IMWG?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Sixty percent clonal marrow plasma cells; Light chain ratio (involved:uninvolved serum free light chain ≥100); MRI showing >1 focal lesion. Any one defines myeloma even without CRAB.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What is the full diagnostic criterion for multiple myeloma?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Clonal bone marrow plasma cells ≥10% (or biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) PLUS at least one myeloma-defining event — a CRAB feature or a SLiM biomarker.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Which investigations replace the skeletal survey for myeloma bone disease?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Whole-body MRI or low-dose whole-body CT (PET-CT also used) — more sensitive than plain skeletal survey. Plus serum/urine electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chains.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: When can the ISTH DIC score be applied?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Only when the patient has an underlying condition known to be associated with DIC (sepsis, malignancy, obstetric emergencies such as abruption or amniotic fluid embolism, major trauma, severe pancreatitis). It is used as an entry criterion, then confirms overt DIC.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the four components of the ISTH DIC score?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Platelet count, elevated fibrin-related marker (D-dimer/FDP), prolonged PT, and fibrinogen level.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What total ISTH DIC score confirms overt DIC, and how often is it repeated?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: A score of ≥5 is compatible with overt DIC and should be repeated daily. A score <5 suggests non-overt DIC and is repeated in 1–2 days.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: State the point bands for each ISTH DIC component.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Platelets: >100=0, 50–100=1, <50=2. Fibrin marker: no rise=0, moderate=2, strong=3. PT prolongation: <3s=0, 3–6s=1, >6s=2. Fibrinogen: >1 g/L=0, <1 g/L=1.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What is the cornerstone of DIC management?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Treat the underlying cause (source control), because DIC is always secondary. Blood products (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen) are given only if the patient is bleeding or at high bleeding risk, not to normalise numbers.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What do the four Ts in the 4T score stand for?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Thrombocytopenia (magnitude of platelet fall), Timing of the platelet fall, Thrombosis (or other sequelae), and oTher cause for thrombocytopenia. Each scores 0, 1 or 2 (max 8).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the 4T score probability bands for HIT?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 0-3 = low probability (HIT unlikely, ~<5%); 4-5 = intermediate; 6-8 = high probability.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What is the pathophysiology of HIT?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: IgG antibodies form against platelet factor 4 (PF4)-heparin complexes, causing platelet activation. This produces a paradoxical PROTHROMBOTIC state with thrombosis despite a falling platelet count.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How is a patient with intermediate/high 4T probability managed?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Stop ALL heparin (including flushes and LMWH), start a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, danaparoid or fondaparinux), and send anti-PF4 ELISA +/- functional assay. Do NOT transfuse platelets; avoid warfarin until platelets recover.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: In HIT, why must platelet transfusions and warfarin be avoided?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: HIT is prothrombotic: platelet transfusions fuel thrombosis. Warfarin before platelet recovery risks venous limb gangrene/skin necrosis, so a non-heparin anticoagulant is used until counts recover.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does the FIGO staging system describe, and what is the unifying I→IV logic across gynae cancers?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: FIGO (Fédération Internationale de Gynécologie et d'Obstétrique) is the international anatomical staging system for gynaecological cancers. Unifying logic: Stage I = confined to organ of origin; II = local/pelvic spread; III = regional/nodal or pelvic sidewall/abdominal spread; IV = distant metastasis or bladder/bowel mucosal invasion. (organ → local → regional → distant)

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How does the STAGING MODALITY differ between cervical, endometrial and ovarian cancer?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Cervical — historically CLINICAL (exam/EUA/colposcopy); the current FIGO revision now incorporates imaging and pathology. Endometrial — SURGICALLY (pathologically) staged at hysterectomy + BSO ± nodes. Ovarian — SURGICALLY staged at laparotomy with washings, omentectomy, biopsies and nodal sampling.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: In FIGO endometrial cancer staging, what distinguishes IA from IB, and what defines Stage II?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Stage I is confined to the uterine body: IA = <50% myometrial invasion, IB = ≥50% myometrial invasion. Stage II = invasion of the cervical stroma but not beyond the uterus.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What FIGO stage is ovarian cancer if there is peritoneal spread outside the pelvis or retroperitoneal nodes? And what defines Stage IV?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Peritoneal spread outside the pelvis and/or retroperitoneal (pelvic/para-aortic) nodes = Stage III. Stage IV = distant metastasis, e.g. pleural effusion with positive cytology (IVA) or liver/splenic parenchymal / extra-abdominal disease (IVB).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Why does ovarian cancer usually present at an advanced FIGO stage, and how should suspicion be acted on?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Symptoms are vague and non-specific — persistent bloating, early satiety, abdominal distension, pelvic/abdominal pain, urinary urgency — so most present at stage III/IV. Maintain a high index of suspicion (especially women ≥50) and investigate with CA-125 and pelvic ultrasound per NICE.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does the MASCC score do in febrile neutropenia, and what is the threshold?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: It risk-stratifies febrile neutropenia into low vs high risk to guide antibiotic route/setting. ≥21 = low risk (consider oral/outpatient antibiotics once stable); <21 = high risk (admit, IV antibiotics). Higher score = lower risk (max 26).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What must happen before you ever calculate a MASCC score in suspected neutropenic sepsis?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Give empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics — piperacillin-tazobactam within 1 hour ("door-to-needle") after taking cultures, without waiting for the neutrophil count. Neutropenic sepsis is an emergency; MASCC is a de-escalation tool used afterwards.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Name the main MASCC components that carry the most weight.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Burden of illness (no/mild symptoms +5, moderate +3), no hypotension (+5), no COPD (+4), solid tumour or no previous fungal infection (+4), no dehydration (+3), outpatient at fever onset (+3), age <60 (+2).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does the Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS) predict, and when is it used?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: A pre-endoscopy score used at first assessment of acute upper GI bleeding. It uses purely clinical parameters and bloods (no endoscopy) to predict the need for intervention (transfusion, endoscopic therapy, surgery) and identifies low-risk patients who may be managed as outpatients. A GBS of 0 (or in some centres ≤1) = very low risk, consider discharge.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: List the components of the Glasgow-Blatchford Score.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Blood urea, haemoglobin (sex-specific thresholds), and systolic BP (all scored in graded bands), plus one-off points for: pulse ≥100, presentation with melaena, presentation with syncope, known hepatic disease, and known cardiac failure. Note there is NO age term and NO endoscopic finding.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does the Rockall score predict, and what is the difference between the clinical and full versions?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Rockall predicts rebleeding and mortality. The pre-endoscopy (clinical) Rockall uses age, shock (pulse/BP) and comorbidity. The full/complete Rockall adds endoscopic findings — the diagnosis and stigmata of recent haemorrhage — and predicts mortality more accurately post-endoscopy. Higher score = higher mortality.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: According to NICE, which score is used at first assessment and which after endoscopy in acute upper GI bleeding?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Use the Glasgow-Blatchford Score at first assessment (front door). Use the full Rockall score after endoscopy to predict rebleeding and mortality.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Why is a raised urea out of proportion to creatinine a clue to an upper GI bleed?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Digested blood in the gut lumen is absorbed like a protein meal, raising blood urea, while renal function (creatinine) remains normal. This disproportionate urea rise is a classic sign of upper GI bleeding and contributes points to the GBS.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does the full (complete) Rockall score predict, and when is it calculated?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: It predicts rebleeding and mortality in acute upper GI bleeding, and is calculated AFTER endoscopy (it needs the diagnosis and stigmata of recent haemorrhage). Range 0-11.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: List the five components of the full Rockall score.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: (1) Age, (2) Shock, (3) Comorbidity, (4) Diagnosis at endoscopy, (5) Stigmata of recent haemorrhage. The first three form the pre-endoscopy (clinical) Rockall (max 7); all five give the full score (max 11).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How are the age and shock components of Rockall scored?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Age: <60 = 0, 60-79 = 1, ≥80 = 2. Shock: no shock (pulse <100, SBP ≥100) = 0; tachycardia (pulse ≥100, SBP ≥100) = 1; hypotension (SBP <100) = 2.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What full Rockall score suggests good prognosis, and what score predicts high mortality?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: A score <3 indicates good prognosis with low rebleed/mortality risk (consider early discharge). A high score, especially ≥8, predicts high mortality.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How does the Glasgow-Blatchford score differ from the full Rockall score?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Glasgow-Blatchford is a PRE-endoscopy tool (clinical + lab data: urea, Hb, SBP, pulse, melaena, syncope, hepatic/cardiac disease) predicting need for INTERVENTION; a score of 0 may allow outpatient management. Full Rockall needs endoscopy findings and predicts rebleeding/mortality.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does the Oakland score assess?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Risk stratification in acute lower GI bleeding (LGIB) — it predicts the probability of a safe discharge (no rebleeding, transfusion, intervention or death), identifying patients suitable for outpatient management.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What Oakland score threshold indicates safe discharge?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: A score of ≤8 predicts a >95% probability of no adverse outcome — consider outpatient management. Scores >8 warrant admission.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Which component carries the biggest weighting in the Oakland score?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Haemoglobin — a low Hb scores heavily (up to ~22 points) and dominates the total (which reaches ~35).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: List the seven components of the Oakland score.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Age, sex (male), previous LGIB admission, blood on DRE, heart rate, systolic BP, and haemoglobin.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Why can a brisk upper GI bleed masquerade as lower GI bleeding?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Rapid intestinal transit can cause an upper GI bleed to present as fresh PR bleeding, often with shock and a raised urea. If unstable, exclude an upper source with OGD regardless of the Oakland score.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What defines SEVERE UC on the Truelove & Witts criteria?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: ≥6 bloody stools per day PLUS ≥1 systemic feature: temperature >37.8°C, pulse >90 bpm, haemoglobin <105 g/L, or ESR >30 mm/hr (or raised CRP). The '6 + 1' rule.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: List the four systemic markers in the Truelove & Witts criteria.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: (1) Temperature >37.8°C; (2) pulse >90 bpm; (3) haemoglobin <105 g/L (anaemia); (4) ESR >30 mm/hr (or CRP raised).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Outline the initial management of acute severe UC (ASUC).
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Admit (medical emergency); IV corticosteroids (hydrocortisone); VTE prophylaxis (LMWH); stool chart & fluid balance; exclude infection (C. difficile, CMV); AXR to exclude toxic megacolon/perforation; daily bloods and observations with joint gastro/surgical input.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the day-3 Travis criteria and why do they matter?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Assessed after 3 days of IV steroids: >8 stools/day, OR CRP >45 with 3–8 stools/day, predicts ~85% need for colectomy. Non-response triggers escalation to rescue therapy (IV ciclosporin or infliximab) or surgery.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Why must antimotility/opioid/antispasmodic drugs be avoided in ASUC?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: They can precipitate or worsen toxic megacolon (colonic dilatation >6 cm + systemic toxicity), which carries a high risk of perforation. Toxic megacolon needs early surgical review and often urgent colectomy.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What condition does the Hinchey classification stage, and using what?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: It stages acute COMPLICATED (perforated) diverticulitis by the extent of contamination, based on CT (contrast abdomen/pelvis) or operative findings. It guides management. Uncomplicated diverticulitis falls outside the classification.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Describe Hinchey stages I and II.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Stage I = pericolic abscess/phlegmon confined to the mesentery/colonic wall (Ia phlegmon, Ib pericolic abscess). Stage II = pelvic, distant intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal abscess (walled-off, remote from the colon).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What is the key difference between Hinchey III and IV?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: III = generalised PURULENT peritonitis (ruptured abscess, no communication with the bowel lumen). IV = generalised FAECULENT peritonitis (free perforation with faecal contamination). III = pus, IV = faeces.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How is a Hinchey I/II abscess managed by size?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Small abscess (≤ 3–4 cm): IV antibiotics alone. Larger abscess (> 3–4 cm): antibiotics PLUS radiological (percutaneous CT-guided) drainage.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What is the management of Hinchey III/IV diverticulitis?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Emergency surgery — classically Hartmann's procedure (sigmoid colectomy + end colostomy) — with resuscitation for sepsis. Laparoscopic lavage is debated (mainly for purulent stage III). Faeculent (IV) peritonitis carries high mortality.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Describe Dukes stages A–D in colorectal cancer.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: A = confined to bowel wall (into but not through muscularis propria); B = through the bowel wall but no nodes; C = regional lymph node involvement (C1 nodes near primary, C2 apical node); D = distant metastasis (e.g. liver). Mnemonic: A in the wall, B through the wall, C in the nodes, D distant.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the approximate 5-year survival figures for Dukes A, B, C and D?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Dukes A ~90%+, Dukes B ~65–70%, Dukes C ~30–40%, Dukes D ~5–10%. Survival worsens progressively with deeper invasion, nodal spread, then distant metastasis.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Define the T stages (Tis–T4) in the TNM staging of colorectal cancer.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Tis = carcinoma in situ; T1 = invades submucosa; T2 = invades muscularis propria; T3 = through muscularis into subserosa/pericolic tissue; T4 = through serosa (T4a) or into adjacent organs (T4b).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How do N stages and stage grouping map to management in colorectal cancer?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: N0 = no nodes, N1 = 1–3 regional nodes, N2 = ≥4 nodes. Stage I = T1–2N0 (≈Dukes A), II = T3–4N0 (≈Dukes B), III = any N+ (≈Dukes C), IV = M1 (≈Dukes D). Stage III (node-positive) warrants adjuvant FOLFOX chemotherapy.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What investigations are used to diagnose and stage colorectal cancer?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Colonoscopy + biopsy for diagnosis; CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for distant staging (liver is commonest met site); MRI rectum for local staging of rectal tumours; CEA as a baseline tumour marker for monitoring. Screening uses the FIT test.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does the Alvarado score estimate and what does its mnemonic stand for?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: It estimates the likelihood of acute appendicitis in a patient with RIF pain. The mnemonic is MANTRELS: Migration of pain, Anorexia, Nausea/vomiting, Tenderness in RIF, Rebound tenderness, Elevated temperature, Leukocytosis, Shift to the left (neutrophilia). Total = 10.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Which two Alvarado components score 2 points each?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Tenderness in the right iliac fossa (T) and Leukocytosis / WCC >10 (L). All other six components score 1 point each.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How do the Alvarado score bands map to management?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 1-4: appendicitis unlikely (consider discharge/alternative diagnosis). 5-6: compatible, observe and/or consider imaging. 7-8: probable, surgical review. 9-10: highly likely, surgical referral.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Why does the Alvarado score have lower specificity in women?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Gynaecological mimics (ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion/cyst, pelvic inflammatory disease) produce overlapping symptoms and signs that raise the score. Always do a pregnancy test to exclude ectopic pregnancy and consider ovarian pathology. Performance is also weaker in children.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Does a low Alvarado score exclude appendicitis?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: No. A low score does not exclude appendicitis, especially early, atypical or retrocaecal presentations. The score supports but does not replace clinical judgement and serial examination; use imaging (USS/CT) or diagnostic laparoscopy when uncertain.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What drug adjuncts are given for a suspected variceal upper GI bleed?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Terlipressin (splanchnic vasoconstrictor) and prophylactic antibiotics (e.g. IV ceftriaxone) at presentation, before endoscopy; definitive treatment is endoscopic band ligation. Antibiotics reduce mortality in variceal bleeding.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: When is a PPI given in a non-variceal (peptic ulcer) upper GI bleed?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: After endoscopic haemostasis of high-risk stigmata — PPIs are not given routinely before endoscopy in NICE guidance. Provide endoscopic dual therapy for active bleeding/visible vessel, then a PPI, and treat H. pylori.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Which endoscopic investigation is used in acute severe ulcerative colitis, and why not colonoscopy?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsy (limited, unprepped) to confirm severity and exclude CMV. Full colonoscopy is avoided in the acute severe setting because of the risk of perforation/toxic megacolon.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does the Glasgow-Imrie score assess, and within what time frame?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: It predicts the SEVERITY of acute pancreatitis (not the diagnosis), using eight variables measured within the first 48 hours of admission.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Recall the PANCREAS mnemonic for the Glasgow-Imrie criteria (each 1 point).
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: PaO₂ <8 kPa; Age >55; Neutrophils (WCC) >15; Calcium <2 mmol/L; Renal (urea) >16 mmol/L; Enzymes (LDH >600 or AST >200); Albumin <32 g/L; Sugar (glucose) >10 mmol/L.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What Glasgow-Imrie score predicts severe pancreatitis, and what should it prompt?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: A score of ≥3 predicts severe pancreatitis and should prompt senior review and consideration of HDU/ITU admission.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Do amylase and lipase levels indicate the severity of pancreatitis?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: No. Amylase/lipase help DIAGNOSE pancreatitis but the degree of rise does NOT correlate with severity. Severity is assessed using scores (Glasgow-Imrie, APACHE II) and CRP >150 at 48h.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Name other tools used to assess acute pancreatitis severity/complications besides Glasgow-Imrie.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Ranson score (US; admission + 48h), APACHE II (generic ICU physiology score, ≥8 = severe, usable any time), CRP >150 at 48h (marker of severity/necrosis), and CT Severity Index (Balthazar) for imaging assessment of necrosis.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the 5 components of the Child-Pugh score (mnemonic)?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: "ABCDE": Albumin, Bilirubin, Clotting (INR/prothrombin time), Distension (ascites) and Encephalopathy. Each is scored 1-3 points, giving a total of 5-15.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How do Child-Pugh classes map to the total score and prognosis?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Class A = 5-6 (well-compensated, ~100% 1-yr survival); Class B = 7-9 (significant compromise); Class C = 10-15 (decompensated, poor prognosis, ~45% 1-yr survival). Higher class = worse survival and higher surgical risk.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What variables make up the MELD score and what is it used for?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Bilirubin, INR and creatinine (MELD-Na adds sodium). It is a calculated logarithmic score (6-40) predicting 3-month mortality, used to prioritise liver transplant allocation - higher MELD = higher priority.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What is the key conceptual difference between Child-Pugh and MELD?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Child-Pugh includes two subjective clinical variables (ascites, encephalopathy) and grades severity/surgical risk at the bedside. MELD is lab-only (objective), predicts short-term mortality, and drives transplant listing.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Which clinical features indicate decompensated cirrhosis and a poor prognosis?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Variceal bleeding, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy and jaundice. These push a patient toward Child-Pugh C / high MELD and should prompt transplant referral, HCC surveillance and a search for reversible precipitants.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What do the King's College Criteria predict, and what decision do they inform?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: They predict poor prognosis in acute liver failure and identify patients who should be referred for urgent liver transplantation. They are a prognostic/referral tool, not a diagnostic one, split into paracetamol and non-paracetamol pathways.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Paracetamol-induced ALF: state the King's criteria for transplant listing.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: List if arterial pH < 7.3 (after adequate fluid resuscitation, > 24 h post-ingestion) OR ALL THREE of: PT > 100 s (INR > 6.5), creatinine > 300 µmol/L, and grade III/IV hepatic encephalopathy. (Some versions add lactate > 3.5 early / > 3.0 after resuscitation.)

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Non-paracetamol ALF: state the King's criteria for transplant listing.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: List if PT > 100 s (INR > 6.5) alone, OR any THREE of five: age < 10 or > 40; aetiology (seronegative hepatitis, drug reaction, halothane); jaundice > 7 days before encephalopathy; PT > 50 s (INR > 3.5); bilirubin > 300 µmol/L.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How is acute liver failure defined, and what is the commonest UK cause?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Hepatic encephalopathy plus coagulopathy (INR > 1.5) in a patient without pre-existing liver disease. Paracetamol overdose is the commonest UK cause.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Outline the management of acute liver failure.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: N-acetylcysteine (give in paracetamol overdose; consider even in non-paracetamol ALF); supportive ITU care; treat cerebral oedema/raised ICP; correct hypoglycaemia; monitor for infection and coagulopathy/bleeding; and discuss EARLY with a liver transplant unit — don't wait for all criteria to be met.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What is the formula for Maddrey's Discriminant Function (DF)?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: DF = 4.6 × (patient PT − control PT) + serum bilirubin (mg/dL). Uses prothrombin time prolongation (in seconds) and bilirubin in mg/dL.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What DF value defines SEVERE alcoholic hepatitis and what does it prompt?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: DF ≥32 = severe alcoholic hepatitis with high 28-day/90-day mortality → consider corticosteroids (prednisolone 40 mg/day) if no contraindication (active infection, GI bleed).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: When is the Lille score calculated and what does it determine?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: At DAY 7 of corticosteroid treatment. It determines RESPONSE to steroids using age, albumin, day-0 bilirubin, change in bilirubin (day 0→7), creatinine and PT.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does a Lille score >0.45 mean and what action follows?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Non-responder — poor prognosis (~75% 6-month mortality). STOP steroids (treatment futile, ongoing infection risk). Lille ≤0.45 = responder, continue steroids.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What must be excluded/treated before starting corticosteroids in alcoholic hepatitis, and name two alternative scores.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Exclude and treat active infection/sepsis and GI bleeding first (steroids worsen sepsis). Alternatives: GAHS (Glasgow Alcoholic Hepatitis Score) and MELD.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does the West Haven criteria grade?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: The severity of hepatic encephalopathy (HE), from Grade 0 (minimal/covert) to Grade 4 (coma).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Distinguish covert vs overt HE by West Haven grade.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Covert = grades 0-1 (subtle/only on psychometric testing). Overt = grades 2-4 (clinically obvious, e.g. disorientation, asterixis, stupor, coma).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the features of West Haven Grade 2?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Lethargy/apathy, disorientation to time, obvious personality change, inappropriate behaviour, asterixis present, dyspraxia (moderate/overt).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Outline the pathophysiology and first-line management of HE.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Failing liver cannot clear ammonia and other gut neurotoxins, causing cerebral dysfunction. First-line: identify and treat the precipitant + lactulose titrated to 2-3 soft stools/day; rifaximin for secondary prevention.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: List key precipitants of hepatic encephalopathy.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Infection/SBP, GI bleeding (protein load), constipation, dehydration/diuretics, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia), sedatives/opioids, high protein load, renal failure, TIPSS.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the three components of Hy's Law?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: (1) Hepatocellular injury with ALT/AST ≥3× ULN, (2) total bilirubin ≥2× ULN, and (3) no other cause and no significant ALP rise (i.e. a hepatocellular, not cholestatic, pattern).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Why does a positive Hy's Law matter clinically?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: It predicts serious drug-induced liver injury with roughly 10% or higher mortality from acute liver failure. The drug should be stopped and the patient escalated; it is a key drug-safety signal in trials.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How is the R ratio calculated and what patterns does it define?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: R = (ALT/ULN) ÷ (ALP/ULN). R ≥5 = hepatocellular (ALT-predominant), R ≤2 = cholestatic (ALP-predominant), 2 < R < 5 = mixed. Hy's Law applies to the hepatocellular pattern.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does RUCAM assess and which domains does it score?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: RUCAM assesses the probability a specific drug caused the liver injury. Domains: time to onset, course after stopping (dechallenge), risk factors (age, alcohol), concomitant drugs, exclusion of other causes, previous hepatotoxicity of the drug, and response to rechallenge. Categories: highly probable / probable / possible / unlikely / excluded.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Name the common culprit drugs in DILI and the key management steps.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Co-amoxiclav (commonest), flucloxacillin, anti-TB drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide), statins, methotrexate, paracetamol (dose-dependent), and herbal/complementary products. Management: STOP the culprit drug, supportive care, monitor LFTs to resolution; NAC for paracetamol.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What three domains does BCLC staging integrate?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Tumour burden (number/size of nodules, vascular invasion, extrahepatic spread), liver function (Child-Pugh class) and performance status (ECOG). It then maps each stage directly to a treatment and prognosis.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: State the Milan criteria for HCC liver transplant eligibility.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: A single tumour ≤5 cm, OR up to 3 tumours each ≤3 cm — with NO extrahepatic spread and NO vascular invasion. Within Milan predicts good post-transplant survival and low recurrence.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Match each BCLC stage (0, A, B, C, D) to its treatment.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 0 (very early) → ablation/resection; A (early) → resection, transplant or ablation (curative); B (intermediate/multinodular) → TACE; C (advanced — vascular invasion/spread or PS 1-2) → systemic therapy; D (terminal — Child-Pugh C or PS 3-4) → best supportive care.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How is HCC screened for and diagnosed in cirrhotics?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Surveillance: 6-monthly liver ultrasound ± AFP in patients with cirrhosis. Diagnosis is often radiological — a nodule with arterial-phase enhancement plus venous/delayed washout on multiphase CT/MRI (LI-RADS) is diagnostic, often avoiding biopsy.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: First-line systemic therapy for advanced (BCLC C) HCC?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Atezolizumab + bevacizumab is first-line. Alternatives/tyrosine kinase inhibitors include sorafenib and lenvatinib. Systemic therapy is used for portal/vascular invasion, extrahepatic spread, or PS 1-2.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does CIWA-Ar assess and how many items does it have?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: It grades the severity of alcohol withdrawal to guide symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing. 10 items (most scored 0-7, orientation 0-4), maximum 67.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What CIWA-Ar score triggers a benzodiazepine dose in a symptom-triggered regimen?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: A score of >=8-10 triggers a benzodiazepine (e.g. chlordiazepoxide, diazepam or lorazepam); the patient is then reassessed and re-scored.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What CIWA-Ar score indicates severe withdrawal with high risk of seizures/DTs?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: >20 = severe withdrawal, high risk of withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens; treat and escalate. (16-20 moderate; 10-15 mild-moderate; <8-10 minimal/mild.)

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Alcohol withdrawal timeline: when do seizures and delirium tremens occur?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Tremor/anxiety 6-12h, alcoholic hallucinosis 12-24h, withdrawal seizures 12-48h, delirium tremens 48-72h (confusion, autonomic instability, hallucinations - medical emergency).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Why is parenteral thiamine given before glucose in alcohol withdrawal, and which benzodiazepine is preferred in liver impairment?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Giving glucose first can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy in a thiamine-deficient patient, so IV thiamine (Pabrinex) goes first. Lorazepam is preferred in significant liver impairment (no active metabolites).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Sepsis-3: define sepsis.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Operationalised as an acute rise in the SOFA score of ≥2 points attributable to infection.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Sepsis-3: define septic shock.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Sepsis with persisting hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg AND a serum lactate >2 mmol/L, despite adequate fluid resuscitation. It identifies a subset with much higher mortality.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the three components of qSOFA (1 point each)?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Respiratory rate ≥22/min, altered mentation (GCS <15), and systolic BP ≤100 mmHg. A score ≥2 flags higher risk of poor outcome and should prompt escalation and assessment for organ dysfunction.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Which six organ systems make up the SOFA score?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Respiration (PaO₂/FiO₂), Coagulation (platelets), Liver (bilirubin), Cardiovascular (MAP/vasopressors), CNS (GCS), and Renal (creatinine/urine output). Each is scored 0–4 (max 24).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: List the Sepsis Six (3 in, 3 out) and the time target.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Deliver within 1 hour. IN: high-flow Oxygen, IV Fluids, IV broad-spectrum Antibiotics. OUT: blood Cultures (before antibiotics), serum Lactate, Urine output monitoring. Mnemonic: BUFALO.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How many parameters does NEWS2 use and what is the score range per parameter?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 7 physiological parameters (respiratory rate, SpO₂, supplemental oxygen, systolic BP, pulse, consciousness/ACVPU, temperature), each scored 0–3, aggregate range 0–20.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What NEWS2 total score triggers sepsis consideration and urgent review?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: A total of ≥5 (MEDIUM or HIGH risk) should trigger sepsis screening/consideration and urgent senior/clinician review.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the two key changes from NEWS1 to NEWS2?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: (1) Addition of SpO₂ Scale 2 for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD), target saturation 88–92%. (2) Consciousness scale changed from AVPU to ACVPU — new-onset Confusion/delirium (C) now scores 3.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How do the NEWS2 risk bands map to escalation?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 0–4 = low (routine, ≥12-hrly obs); any single parameter =3 (red) = urgent clinician review, hourly obs; 5–6 = medium (urgent review, consider sepsis, hourly obs); ≥7 = high (emergency critical-care assessment, continuous monitoring).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: When should SpO₂ Scale 2 be used in NEWS2 and what is the caveat?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Only in patients with confirmed risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (e.g. COPD), on a senior clinical decision, with a target of 88–92%. Do not over-oxygenate; default to Scale 1 (target 96%) otherwise.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What blood volume and percentage loss define ATLS Class I vs Class IV haemorrhage (70 kg adult)?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Class I: <15% loss (<750 mL). Class IV: >40% loss (>2000 mL). Circulating volume assumed ~5 L in a 70 kg adult, so each ~15% ≈ 750 mL.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Which vital sign changes are the EARLIEST reliable signs of haemorrhage in ATLS classes?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Tachycardia and a NARROWED pulse pressure (raised diastolic from compensatory vasoconstriction) appear in Class II, before any fall in systolic BP. They precede hypotension.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: At which ATLS class does systolic blood pressure first fall, and why does this matter?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Systolic BP falls in Class III (30–40%, 1500–2000 mL loss). Hypotension is therefore a LATE sign — fit young patients compensate and maintain BP until then, so a normal BP does not exclude major blood loss.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Give the heart rate, respiratory rate and urine output for ATLS Class III haemorrhage.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Class III (30–40%, 1500–2000 mL): HR 120–140, RR 30–40, urine output 5–15 mL/hr, decreased systolic BP, narrowed pulse pressure, anxious/confused.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the key management steps for significant haemorrhagic shock (ATLS Class III/IV)?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Control the haemorrhage (pressure/tourniquet/splint/surgery), two large-bore IV cannulae, activate major haemorrhage protocol with balanced blood product resuscitation, permissive hypotension in trauma, tranexamic acid within 3 hours, and treat the source.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the three components of the MUST score?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 1) BMI, 2) Unplanned weight loss over 3-6 months, and 3) Acute disease effect (no/likely no nutritional intake for >5 days in an acutely ill patient). The three are scored and summed.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How is BMI scored in MUST?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: BMI >20 kg/m² = 0 points; BMI 18.5-20 = 1 point; BMI <18.5 = 2 points.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How is unplanned weight loss scored in MUST?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Weight loss over 3-6 months: <5% = 0 points; 5-10% = 1 point; >10% = 2 points.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What do the total MUST scores mean and what action follows?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 0 = low risk (routine care, repeat screening); 1 = medium risk (observe, document intake for 3 days, repeat screening); ≥2 = high risk (treat - refer to dietitian/nutrition support team, set goals, monitor).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What is refeeding syndrome and how is it prevented?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: A dangerous fluid/electrolyte shift when feeding is reintroduced in at-risk patients (little/no intake >5 days, low BMI, alcohol excess). Features hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and thiamine deficiency. Prevent by starting feed slowly (~10 kcal/kg/day), giving thiamine/B vitamins before feeding, replacing phosphate/potassium/magnesium, and monitoring electrolytes.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: In which direction does the Waterlow score run, and what are the risk bands?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Higher score = higher risk. Waterlow ≥10 = at risk, ≥15 = high risk, ≥20 = very high risk.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: In which direction does the Braden scale run, and what are the bands?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: LOWER score = HIGHER risk (opposite to Waterlow). ≤9 very high, 10–12 high, 13–14 moderate, 15–18 mild, 19–23 low. Total range 6–23.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the 6 Braden subscales?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, and friction/shear.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does the SSKIN prevention bundle stand for?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Surface (pressure-redistributing mattress/cushion), Skin inspection (regular), Keep moving (reposition, e.g. 2-hourly), Incontinence/moisture management, Nutrition/hydration.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Describe EPUAP/NPUAP pressure ulcer categories 1–4.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 1 = non-blanching erythema of intact skin; 2 = partial-thickness loss/blister; 3 = full-thickness skin loss (subcutaneous fat visible); 4 = full-thickness tissue loss (muscle/tendon/bone exposed). Plus unstageable and deep tissue injury.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the three components of the GCS and their maximum scores?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Eye opening (E, /4), Verbal response (V, /5), Motor response (M, /6). Summed for a total of 3 (min) to 15 (max).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How do you score EYE opening on the GCS?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 4 = spontaneous; 3 = to speech/sound; 2 = to pain/pressure; 1 = none.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How do you score the MOTOR response on the GCS?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 6 = obeys commands; 5 = localises to pain; 4 = normal flexion (withdraws); 3 = abnormal flexion (decorticate); 2 = extension (decerebrate); 1 = none. Motor is the most prognostically important component.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What GCS bands define mild, moderate and severe brain injury, and what is the airway rule?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 13-15 mild, 9-12 moderate, ≤8 severe. GCS ≤8 → the patient cannot protect their airway → consider intubation ('GCS 8, intubate').

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What is AVPU and how does it relate to GCS?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: A simpler bedside screen: Alert / responds to Voice / responds to Pain / Unresponsive. 'P' (responds only to pain) corresponds roughly to a GCS of 8.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does the Apfel score predict?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: The risk of post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV) within 24 hours in adults having general anaesthesia. It uses four risk factors to stratify risk and guide antiemetic prophylaxis.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: List the four Apfel risk factors (each 1 point).
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 1) Female sex; 2) Non-smoker; 3) History of PONV or motion sickness; 4) Anticipated post-operative opioid use. Maximum score = 4.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Map Apfel score 0–4 to approximate PONV risk.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 0 pts ~10%, 1 pt ~20%, 2 pts ~40%, 3 pts ~60%, 4 pts ~80%. Each point roughly steps the risk up by ~20%.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Name antiemetics by class used for PONV prophylaxis.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Ondansetron (5-HT₃ antagonist), dexamethasone (corticosteroid), cyclizine (antihistamine), prochlorperazine/droperidol (dopamine D₂ antagonist), aprepitant (NK₁ antagonist). Combine different classes for higher risk.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Which baseline anaesthetic strategies reduce PONV risk?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Regional anaesthesia where possible, avoid volatiles and nitrous oxide, use propofol TIVA, minimise opioids (opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia), and ensure adequate hydration.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does the ASA Physical Status classification grade?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: A patient's baseline systemic health and fitness for anaesthesia (physical status), assigned pre-operatively. It grades the patient, NOT the operation, and does not by itself account for surgery type or airway difficulty.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Distinguish ASA II from ASA III.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: ASA II = mild systemic disease with NO substantive functional limitation (e.g. smoker, well-controlled DM/HTN, BMI 30–40, pregnancy). ASA III = severe systemic disease WITH substantive functional limitation (e.g. COPD, poorly-controlled DM/HTN, BMI ≥40, ESRD on dialysis, MI/CVA/stent >3 months ago).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Define ASA IV, V and VI.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: ASA IV = severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life (e.g. recent <3-month MI/CVA/stent, sepsis, DIC, ESRD not on dialysis). ASA V = moribund patient not expected to survive without the operation (e.g. ruptured AAA, massive trauma). ASA VI = declared brain-dead patient for organ donation.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does the 'E' suffix mean in an ASA grade?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Emergency surgery — where delay would significantly increase the threat to life or a body part (e.g. ASA IIIE). It independently signifies higher perioperative risk.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Where does a well-controlled diabetic on treatment, and a poorly-controlled diabetic, each sit on ASA?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Well-controlled diabetes = ASA II (mild disease, no functional limitation). Poorly-controlled diabetes = ASA III (severe disease with functional limitation).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the three steps of the WHO analgesic ladder?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Step 1: non-opioid (paracetamol and/or NSAID) ± adjuvant. Step 2: weak opioid (codeine, dihydrocodeine, tramadol) + non-opioid ± adjuvant. Step 3: strong opioid (morphine first-line, oxycodone, fentanyl, buprenorphine) + non-opioid ± adjuvant.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What do the three 'by's of the WHO ladder stand for?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: By the mouth (oral route preferred), by the clock (regular fixed-interval dosing, not just PRN), and by the ladder (start at the step matching severity, titrate up if pain persists and down as it improves).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How is a breakthrough (PRN) opioid dose calculated?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Roughly 1/6 of the total 24-hour opioid dose, given as needed for breakthrough pain in addition to the regular background dose.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Which adjuvants are used for neuropathic pain, and at which step?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin and pregabalin. Adjuvants can be added at ANY step of the ladder. Other adjuvants include corticosteroids, bisphosphonates (bone pain) and antispasmodics.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Why is morphine avoided in renal impairment, and what are the signs of opioid toxicity?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Morphine has renally-excreted active metabolites that accumulate (causing sedation/myoclonus); use oxycodone, alfentanil or buprenorphine instead. Toxicity triad: pinpoint pupils, drowsiness/sedation, reduced respiratory rate — reverse with naloxone.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What does the AEIOU mnemonic stand for?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: The emergency indications for renal replacement therapy (RRT) in AKI: A = Acidosis (severe, refractory metabolic acidosis), E = Electrolytes (refractory hyperkalaemia), I = Intoxication (dialysable toxins/drugs), O = Overload (refractory fluid overload/pulmonary oedema), U = Uraemia (encephalopathy, pericarditis, bleeding).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: In AEIOU, what is the acidosis threshold and key qualifier for RRT?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Severe metabolic acidosis, e.g. pH <7.1–7.2, that is refractory to medical treatment (fluids, treating the underlying cause, considering bicarbonate). The qualifier 'refractory' applies to all five AEIOU indications.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Which toxins/drugs are dialysable ('I' for Intoxication) — give the BLAST mnemonic.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: BLAST: Barbiturates, Lithium, Alcohols (methanol, ethylene glycol), Salicylates/aspirin, Theophylline. Metformin (causing lactic acidosis) is another important dialysable drug.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the uraemic emergency indications for RRT ('U' in AEIOU)?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Symptomatic/severe uraemia: uraemic encephalopathy, uraemic pericarditis (pericardial rub), uraemic bleeding, or a very high urea. Pericarditis and encephalopathy are urgent indications.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: When is CRRT preferred over intermittent haemodialysis in AKI?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT/haemofiltration) is preferred for haemodynamically unstable patients, typically in ITU, because it removes fluid and solute more slowly and gently. Intermittent haemodialysis suits the haemodynamically stable patient.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: How is the IPSS structured and what is the total score range?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Seven LUTS symptom questions, each scored 0-5 (not at all to almost always), giving a total of 0-35. There is also a separate 8th quality-of-life ('bother') question scored 0-6 (delighted to terrible), which is reported alongside but not added to the total.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the IPSS severity bands?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: 0-7 = mild; 8-19 = moderate; 20-35 = severe. Bands guide the intensity of management and provide a baseline for monitoring treatment response.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Which LUTS are 'storage/irritative' vs 'voiding/obstructive'?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Storage/irritative: frequency, urgency, nocturia. Voiding/obstructive: weak stream, straining, intermittency, incomplete emptying. Distinguishing them helps guide treatment (e.g. anticholinergic/mirabegron for storage symptoms).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Compare tamsulosin and finasteride in BPH LUTS.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Tamsulosin (alpha-blocker) relaxes prostatic smooth muscle for rapid symptom relief; caution postural hypotension. Finasteride (5-alpha-reductase inhibitor) shrinks the prostate over months, is best for larger glands, and lowers PSA (roughly halves it).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What red flags must be excluded before attributing LUTS to BPH?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Haematuria, recurrent UTI, palpable bladder/retention, renal impairment, and an abnormal (hard/nodular) DRE which warrants a 2-week-wait referral for suspected prostate cancer. Rule out UTI first. Acute urinary retention is an emergency requiring catheterisation.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What imaging feature is the key discriminator in the Bosniak classification?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Enhancement (measurable contrast uptake, generally a rise of ≥15 HU). It indicates vascularity and pushes a cystic renal lesion into a higher category (III/IV), raising malignant risk and prompting surgery.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are Bosniak categories I and II, and how are they managed?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: I = simple benign cyst (thin hairline wall, water density, no enhancement, ~0% malignant). II = minimally complex benign (few thin septa, fine calcification, or ≤3cm hyperdense non-enhancing cyst). Both are benign and need no follow-up.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What is a Bosniak IIF lesion and how is it managed?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: IIF (F = follow-up): multiple thin septa, minimal smooth wall/septal thickening, or thicker/nodular calcification — all non-enhancing. ~5–10% malignant. Managed with surveillance imaging; must NOT be discharged.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: Compare Bosniak categories III and IV.
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: III = indeterminate, thick/irregular walls or septa with measurable enhancement (~50% malignant). IV = enhancing soft-tissue/solid components adjacent to but independent of the wall/septa (~90%+ malignant). Both are managed with surgical resection.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What malignancy work-up follows a suspicious (III/IV) cystic renal lesion, and the commonest histology?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.back: Full renal cell carcinoma work-up including staging CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis. Most renal cancers are clear cell RCC. Management is typically surgical resection / (partial) nephrectomy.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.front: What are the six IMDC (Heng) risk factors for metastatic RCC?
