investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A haemodynamically stable patient has a Hinchey II diverticular abscess measuring 6 cm on CT. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Conservative management with oral antibiotics at home
IV antibiotics alone with no drainage
Elective sigmoid colectomy the same week
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Antibiotics plus percutaneous (radiological) drainage
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: A Hinchey I/II abscess larger than roughly 3–4 cm is managed with antibiotics plus radiological percutaneous drainage. Abscesses ≤ 3–4 cm can often be treated with antibiotics alone. Emergency surgery is reserved for Hinchey III/IV (generalised peritonitis).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which statement about the Hinchey classification is correct?
options: Stage IV (faeculent peritonitis) carries a high mortality and mandates urgent surgery
It is a probability score predicting the risk of developing diverticulitis
The staging investigation of choice is colonoscopy during the acute episode
Stage I disease routinely requires emergency Hartmann's procedure
It applies mainly to uncomplicated diverticulitis
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Stage IV (faeculent peritonitis) carries a high mortality and mandates urgent surgery
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Hinchey IV is free perforation with faecal peritonitis, carrying high mortality and requiring resuscitation plus urgent surgery. Hinchey is an anatomical severity grade (not a predictive probability score); CT (not acute colonoscopy) is the staging investigation; it applies to COMPLICATED disease; and stage I is managed non-operatively.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A colorectal tumour has invaded through the bowel wall breaching the serosa but there is no lymph node involvement and no distant spread. What is the Dukes stage and approximate 5-year survival?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Dukes B, ~65–70%
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Dukes B is tumour that has penetrated through the bowel wall (breaching muscularis propria/serosa) but without lymph node involvement, carrying roughly a 65–70% 5-year survival. Dukes A is confined within the wall (~90%), and node involvement would make it Dukes C.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient's staging shows T3 N1 M0 colorectal cancer. Which stage group and adjuvant treatment is most appropriate?
options: Stage III; surgery plus adjuvant FOLFOX chemotherapy
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Stage III; surgery plus adjuvant FOLFOX chemotherapy
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: N1 indicates 1–3 involved regional nodes, so any node-positive disease (N1 or N2) with M0 is Stage III, corresponding to Dukes C. Standard management is surgical resection plus adjuvant FOLFOX chemotherapy for node-positive disease.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: In the TNM staging of colorectal cancer, what does N2 signify?
options: 4 or more regional lymph nodes involved
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: 4 or more regional lymph nodes involved
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: N0 = no regional nodes, N1 = 1–3 regional nodes, and N2 = 4 or more regional nodes. Distant spread is captured by the M category (M1), not N, and any node-positive disease places the tumour at least at Stage III.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 22-year-old man has RIF tenderness, migration of pain to the RIF, anorexia, and a WCC of 14 x10^9/L. Which single feature contributes the most points to his Alvarado score alongside leukocytosis?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Tenderness in the RIF
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Tenderness in the RIF (T) scores 2 points, as does Leukocytosis (L). These are the two most heavily weighted components. Migration, anorexia, rebound and elevated temperature each score only 1 point.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient scores 3 on the Alvarado score. What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?
options: Appendicitis unlikely, consider discharge or an alternative diagnosis
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Appendicitis unlikely, consider discharge or an alternative diagnosis
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: A score of 1-4 indicates appendicitis is unlikely, so discharge or pursuit of an alternative diagnosis is reasonable. However, a low score does not exclude appendicitis, and serial examination should be used if concern persists.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 24-year-old woman presents with RIF pain and an Alvarado score of 6. Which action is most important before attributing her symptoms to appendicitis?
options: Perform a pregnancy test to exclude ectopic pregnancy
Repeat the Alvarado score in 24 hours only
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Perform a pregnancy test to exclude ectopic pregnancy
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The Alvarado score has lower specificity in women because gynaecological conditions mimic appendicitis. A pregnancy test is essential to exclude ectopic pregnancy, and ovarian pathology should be considered. Imaging (USS/CT) or diagnostic laparoscopy may be needed where uncertainty remains.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient with known cirrhosis presents with haematemesis and suspected variceal bleeding. Alongside resuscitation, what drug treatment should be started before endoscopy?
options: No drugs until endoscopy is performed
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Suspected variceal bleeding warrants terlipressin (splanchnic vasoconstrictor) plus prophylactic antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone) at presentation, before endoscopic band ligation. Prophylactic antibiotics reduce mortality; a PPI is used for non-variceal ulcer bleeding after endoscopic haemostasis.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient with acute severe ulcerative colitis needs endoscopic confirmation. Which investigation is most appropriate?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsy
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: A limited, unprepped flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsy confirms severity and excludes CMV in acute severe UC. Full colonoscopy is avoided acutely because of the perforation/toxic megacolon risk; barium enema is contraindicated in severe colitis.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 60-year-old man is admitted with acute pancreatitis. Which set of results scores a point on the Glasgow-Imrie score?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Urea 20 mmol/L
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The renal criterion scores when urea >16 mmol/L, so urea 20 scores a point. The other values are all within the non-scoring range: calcium scores if <2, albumin if <32, PaO₂ if <8 kPa, and WCC/neutrophils if >15.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which statement about assessing acute pancreatitis severity is correct?
options: A very high amylase reliably indicates severe disease
A Glasgow-Imrie score ≥3 predicts severe pancreatitis
APACHE II can only be calculated at exactly 48 hours
Lipase level determines the need for ITU
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: A Glasgow-Imrie score ≥3 predicts severe pancreatitis
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Glasgow-Imrie ≥3 predicts severe disease and prompts HDU/ITU consideration. The magnitude of amylase/lipase rise does not reflect severity. APACHE II is a generic physiology score usable at any time, and it is CRP >150 (not <150) at 48h that marks severity/necrosis.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which is the most important early intervention in a patient with predicted severe acute pancreatitis?
options: Immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics for all patients
Withholding all analgesia to monitor pain
Routine immediate ERCP regardless of cause
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Early aggressive IV fluid resuscitation
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Early aggressive IV fluid resuscitation is the mainstay of management, alongside analgesia, monitoring and treating the cause. Antibiotics are not routine, surgery is not first-line, analgesia should be given, and ERCP is reserved for obstructing gallstones/cholangitis rather than all-comers.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which set of parameters is used to calculate the MELD score?
options: Albumin, bilirubin, INR, ascites and encephalopathy
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Bilirubin, INR and creatinine (± sodium)
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: MELD uses bilirubin, INR and creatinine, with MELD-Na additionally incorporating serum sodium. These are all objective laboratory values, in contrast to Child-Pugh which also includes the subjective clinical variables of ascites and encephalopathy.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A cirrhotic patient has a Child-Pugh total score of 11. Which class is this and what does it indicate?
options: Class C - decompensated disease with poor prognosis
Score is invalid; maximum Child-Pugh is 10
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Class C - decompensated disease with poor prognosis
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Child-Pugh totals run from 5 to 15: Class A = 5-6, Class B = 7-9, Class C = 10-15. A score of 11 is Class C, indicating decompensated cirrhosis, poor 1- and 2-year survival, high peri-operative mortality, and a patient in whom transplant should be considered.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: What is the primary clinical use of the MELD score?
options: Diagnosing cirrhosis on a liver biopsy
Grading the severity of acute pancreatitis
Prioritising patients for liver transplant allocation
Predicting the risk of variceal bleeding alone
Deciding antibiotic choice in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Prioritising patients for liver transplant allocation
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: MELD predicts 3-month mortality in end-stage liver disease and is used to rank patients on the transplant waiting list - a higher MELD reflects a sicker patient with greater short-term mortality and therefore higher transplant priority. It does not diagnose cirrhosis or guide antibiotic choice.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 25-year-old is admitted 30 hours after a staggered paracetamol overdose. After adequate fluid resuscitation, the arterial pH is 7.24. Which King's College Criterion has been met?
options: None — a single abnormal value can never meet the criteria
Arterial pH < 7.3, which alone meets the paracetamol criteria for transplant listing
PT > 100 s, which alone meets the paracetamol criteria
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Arterial pH < 7.3, which alone meets the paracetamol criteria for transplant listing
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: In the paracetamol pathway, an arterial pH < 7.3 (after adequate fluid resuscitation and > 24 h post-ingestion) is by itself sufficient to meet the King's Criteria for transplant referral, independent of the PT/creatinine/encephalopathy triad.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: In the PARACETAMOL-induced pathway, which combination (in the absence of significant acidosis) meets the King's College Criteria for transplant?
options: Any one of: PT > 100 s, creatinine > 300 µmol/L, or grade III/IV encephalopathy
PT > 100 s (INR > 6.5) AND creatinine > 300 µmol/L AND grade III/IV encephalopathy — all three together
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: PT > 100 s (INR > 6.5) AND creatinine > 300 µmol/L AND grade III/IV encephalopathy — all three together
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The paracetamol triad requires ALL THREE of PT > 100 s (INR > 6.5), creatinine > 300 µmol/L, and grade III/IV encephalopathy simultaneously. Any single component alone is insufficient. The alternative single-criterion route is arterial pH < 7.3.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which statement about acute liver failure and the King's College Criteria is correct?
options: N-acetylcysteine should only ever be given in paracetamol-related ALF
Referral to a transplant centre should be delayed until all criteria are definitively met
The criteria are highly sensitive, so a patient not meeting them is safe from death
The INR should be aggressively corrected as soon as ALF is diagnosed
ALF is defined as encephalopathy plus coagulopathy (INR > 1.5) without pre-existing liver disease, and referral should be early
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: ALF is defined as encephalopathy plus coagulopathy (INR > 1.5) without pre-existing liver disease, and referral should be early
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: ALF is encephalopathy + coagulopathy (INR > 1.5) in a previously normal liver. Refer early rather than waiting for all criteria; NAC is considered even in non-paracetamol ALF; the criteria are specific but not perfectly sensitive; and the INR is a prognostic marker not routinely corrected.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 52-year-old man with jaundice and heavy alcohol use has a prothrombin time 8 seconds above control and a bilirubin of 12 mg/dL. What is his Maddrey Discriminant Function and what does it indicate?
options: DF = 92 — severe, but steroids contraindicated by the score itself
DF cannot be calculated without the MELD score
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: DF = 48.8 — severe, consider corticosteroids
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: DF = 4.6 × (8) + 12 = 36.8 + 12 = 48.8. A DF ≥32 defines severe alcoholic hepatitis with high short-term mortality, prompting consideration of prednisolone 40 mg/day once infection and GI bleeding are excluded/treated.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient with severe alcoholic hepatitis has been on prednisolone for 7 days. Their Lille score is 0.62. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Continue steroids for the full 28 days as planned
Increase the prednisolone dose to 60 mg
Stop corticosteroids as the patient is a non-responder
Recalculate the Maddrey DF and restart therapy
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Stop corticosteroids as the patient is a non-responder
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: A Lille score >0.45 at day 7 identifies a non-responder with roughly 75% 6-month mortality. Continuing steroids is futile and prolongs infection risk, so they should be stopped; transplant assessment or palliation may be considered.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which statement best captures how the Maddrey DF and Lille score are used together in severe alcoholic hepatitis?
options: Both are calculated at presentation and averaged to give a single risk score
DF is used at day 7 and Lille at presentation
DF selects who to start on steroids; Lille at day 7 assesses whether steroids are working
Lille replaces the DF entirely and is calculated at admission
Both scores require liver biopsy before they can be applied
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: DF selects who to start on steroids; Lille at day 7 assesses whether steroids are working
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Maddrey DF ≥32 at presentation identifies severe disease and selects candidates for corticosteroids, while the Lille score calculated after 7 days of treatment gauges response — >0.45 indicates non-response and steroids should be stopped.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient with cirrhosis is lethargic, disorientated to time, has an obvious personality change and demonstrable asterixis, but is rousable and follows simple commands. What is the West Haven grade?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Grade 2
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Lethargy/apathy, disorientation to time, obvious personality change and asterixis define Grade 2 (moderate, overt HE). Grade 1 is only trivial lack of awareness; Grade 3 involves somnolence/semi-stupor with gross disorientation.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A cirrhotic patient presents with new-onset overt hepatic encephalopathy. Which is the single most important initial step in management?
options: Identify and treat the precipitating cause
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Identify and treat the precipitating cause
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: HE is almost always precipitated (infection/SBP, GI bleed, constipation, electrolyte disturbance, sedatives, etc.). Finding and treating the trigger is paramount, alongside lactulose. Prolonged protein restriction is harmful, and rifaximin is used for prevention of recurrence rather than as sole acute therapy.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which statement about the West Haven grading of hepatic encephalopathy is correct?
options: Grade 0 is diagnosed on routine bedside examination
Grade 4 patients remain responsive to painful stimuli
Asterixis is characteristic of Grade 4 coma
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Grades 2-4 constitute overt HE
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Grades 2-4 are overt (clinically obvious); grades 0-1 are covert. Grade 0 (minimal HE) is detectable only on psychometric testing. Grade 4 is coma, unresponsive to pain/stimuli. Asterixis is a feature of milder overt grades (1-2), not grade 4.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient on a new drug has ALT 4× ULN, total bilirubin 3× ULN, normal ALP, and an ultrasound showing no biliary obstruction, with negative viral and autoimmune screens. Which statement is correct?
options: This is cholestatic injury and Hy's Law does not apply
This meets Hy's Law and predicts high risk of serious DILI
The drug can be safely continued with monitoring
Bilirubin is irrelevant to Hy's Law
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: This meets Hy's Law and predicts high risk of serious DILI
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: ALT ≥3× ULN plus bilirubin ≥2× ULN, in a hepatocellular pattern (normal ALP) with other causes excluded, is Hy's Law positive — roughly 10%+ mortality. The drug should be stopped and the patient escalated.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient has ALT 8× ULN and ALP 8× ULN. What is the R ratio and injury pattern?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: R = 1, cholestatic
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: R = (ALT/ULN) ÷ (ALP/ULN) = 8 ÷ 8 = 1. An R ≤2 defines a cholestatic (ALP-predominant) pattern, to which Hy's Law does not apply.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which statement about RUCAM is correct?
options: It measures the severity and mortality of liver injury
It replaces the need to stop the culprit drug
It scores the probability that a specific drug caused the liver injury
It only applies to paracetamol toxicity
It is identical to Hy's Law
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: It scores the probability that a specific drug caused the liver injury
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: RUCAM is a structured causality tool giving categories from highly probable to excluded, scoring time to onset, dechallenge, risk factors, concomitant drugs, exclusion of other causes, known hepatotoxicity, and rechallenge. Hy's Law, by contrast, grades severity/prognosis.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 61-year-old with hepatitis C cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A, ECOG PS 0) has a single 4 cm HCC on MRI, no vascular invasion and no extrahepatic disease. Which statement about transplant eligibility is correct?
options: Outside Milan — the lesion exceeds 3 cm
Within Milan — a single lesion ≤5 cm with no invasion or spread
Outside Milan — transplant is never offered for a single lesion
Within Milan only if AFP is normal
Outside Milan — he must have ≤3 lesions to qualify
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Within Milan — a single lesion ≤5 cm with no invasion or spread
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Milan criteria allow a single tumour up to 5 cm (or up to 3 nodules each ≤3 cm) provided there is no vascular invasion and no extrahepatic spread. A solitary 4 cm lesion with no spread is comfortably within Milan, so he is transplant-eligible.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A cirrhotic patient has multinodular HCC confined to the liver, Child-Pugh A, ECOG PS 0, with no vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread. What is the BCLC stage and recommended treatment?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Stage B — transarterial chemoembolisation (TACE)
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Intermediate-stage HCC (BCLC B) is multinodular disease with preserved liver function and PS 0, without vascular invasion or spread. The standard treatment is TACE.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which single feature would move an otherwise early-stage HCC into BCLC stage C (advanced)?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Portal vein (vascular) invasion
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: BCLC stage C (advanced) is defined by macrovascular/portal invasion, extrahepatic spread, or performance status 1-2, and is treated with systemic therapy (e.g. atezolizumab + bevacizumab). Vascular invasion also places a tumour outside the Milan criteria for transplant.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 52-year-old man admitted with alcohol dependence is being monitored on a symptom-triggered regimen. His CIWA-Ar score is 12. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Withhold all medication and reassess in 24 hours
Give a benzodiazepine dose and reassess/re-score
Give IV glucose before anything else
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Give a benzodiazepine dose and reassess/re-score
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: A CIWA-Ar >=8-10 triggers a benzodiazepine dose in a symptom-triggered regimen. A score of 12 is above threshold, so a benzodiazepine (e.g. chlordiazepoxide) is given and the patient re-scored to titrate further doses.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which CIWA-Ar band indicates severe withdrawal with the highest risk of seizures and delirium tremens?
options: Any score with a normal orientation item
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: A CIWA-Ar >20 indicates severe withdrawal with a high risk of withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens, mandating treatment and escalation. 16-20 is moderate, 10-15 mild-moderate, and <8-10 minimal/mild.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A malnourished alcohol-dependent patient presents drowsy and hypoglycaemic. What is the key principle regarding thiamine and glucose administration?
options: Give IV glucose immediately, thiamine can wait days
Give parenteral thiamine before administering glucose
Never give thiamine in alcohol withdrawal
Give oral thiamine only, glucose is contraindicated
Thiamine and glucose must never be given to the same patient
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Give parenteral thiamine before administering glucose
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Administering glucose to a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy. Parenteral thiamine (IV Pabrinex) must be given before or with glucose to prevent this.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 68-year-old with a chest infection has RR 24, is newly confused (GCS 14), and has a systolic BP of 98 mmHg. What is his qSOFA score and the appropriate interpretation?
options: 3 — high risk of poor outcome, escalate and assess for organ dysfunction
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: 3 — high risk of poor outcome, escalate and assess for organ dysfunction
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: All three qSOFA criteria are met: RR ≥22 (1), altered mentation/GCS <15 (1), and SBP ≤100 (1), giving a score of 3. A qSOFA ≥2 identifies a patient at higher risk of poor outcome and should prompt escalation and assessment for organ dysfunction. qSOFA itself does not confirm sepsis or diagnose septic shock — those require organ dysfunction (SOFA ≥2) and the vasopressor-plus-lactate criteria respectively.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: According to Sepsis-3, which combination defines septic shock?
options: Lactate >2 mmol/L on admission before any fluids
Vasopressors required to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg AND lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation
Systolic BP <90 mmHg that responds to a single fluid bolus
A SOFA score of ≥2 in a patient with infection
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Vasopressors required to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg AND lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Septic shock is sepsis with circulatory and cellular/metabolic dysfunction: persisting hypotension needing vasopressors to keep MAP ≥65 mmHg AND lactate >2 mmol/L, both despite adequate fluid resuscitation. A SOFA rise ≥2 with infection defines sepsis, not shock. Lactate before fluids or a fluid-responsive BP does not meet the shock definition.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which statement about the Sepsis Six is correct?
options: Broad-spectrum antibiotics should be given before taking blood cultures to avoid delay
The bundle should be completed within 6 hours of recognition
Blood cultures should be taken before antibiotics, and the whole bundle delivered within 1 hour
Oxygen is withheld until the lactate result is available
Urine output monitoring is optional and only for patients already in shock
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Blood cultures should be taken before antibiotics, and the whole bundle delivered within 1 hour
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The Sepsis Six is delivered within the first hour ('golden hour'). Blood cultures are taken before antibiotics to maximise diagnostic yield, then broad-spectrum IV antibiotics are given. The 'three in' are oxygen, IV fluids and IV antibiotics; the 'three out' are cultures, lactate and urine output. Oxygen is given promptly (not delayed for lactate), and urine output monitoring is a core part of the bundle for all patients, not optional.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 68-year-old man with a productive cough has: RR 22, SpO₂ 95% on air, BP 108/70, pulse 105, temperature 38.4°C, alert. His NEWS2 aggregate is 6. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Urgent review by a clinician and active consideration of sepsis
No escalation as no single parameter scores 3
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Urgent review by a clinician and active consideration of sepsis
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: A NEWS2 total of 5–6 is the MEDIUM band and, in a patient with suspected infection, ≥5 is the recommended trigger to screen for and consider sepsis with urgent clinician review and at least hourly observations.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which parameter change is unique to NEWS2 compared with the original NEWS?
options: Adding respiratory rate to the score
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Scoring new-onset confusion (ACVPU 'C') as 3
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: NEWS2 replaced AVPU with ACVPU so that new confusion/delirium (C) scores 3. Respiratory rate, systolic BP, temperature and supplemental oxygen were all already part of the original NEWS.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: For which patient group is the NEWS2 SpO₂ Scale 2 (target 88–92%) intended?
options: Patients with confirmed risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, e.g. COPD, on senior decision
Any patient with a SpO₂ below 96%
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Patients with confirmed risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, e.g. COPD, on senior decision
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Scale 2 is reserved for patients with a confirmed or prior risk of type 2 (hypercapnic) respiratory failure, typically COPD, and should be applied only on a senior clinical decision with a target of 88–92% to avoid over-oxygenation. All other patients use Scale 1 (target 96%).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 25-year-old man is brought in after a stabbing. HR 110, systolic BP 122 mmHg, diastolic 95 mmHg, RR 24, urine output 25 mL/hr, mildly anxious. Which ATLS haemorrhage class best fits, and what is the key finding?
options: Class I — he is fully compensated with normal vitals
Class II — tachycardia with a narrowed pulse pressure but preserved systolic BP
Class III — decompensated with a falling systolic BP
Class IV — peri-arrest with negligible urine output
Not classifiable because his systolic BP is normal
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Class II — tachycardia with a narrowed pulse pressure but preserved systolic BP
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: HR 100–120, systolic BP still normal but pulse pressure narrowed by a raised diastolic (95 mmHg), RR 20–30 and urine 20–30 mL/hr define Class II (15–30% loss). The narrowed pulse pressure with a normal systolic is the classic early tell — reflecting ~750–1500 mL loss despite a 'reassuring' blood pressure.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Why can a fit young trauma patient have a normal systolic blood pressure despite significant haemorrhage?
options: Blood loss under 40% never affects any vital sign
Compensatory vasoconstriction maintains systolic BP until roughly Class III (30–40% loss), making hypotension a late sign
Systolic BP rises with blood loss due to catecholamines
Pulse pressure widens early and protects the systolic reading
Urine output increases to compensate for lost volume
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Compensatory vasoconstriction maintains systolic BP until roughly Class III (30–40% loss), making hypotension a late sign
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Young, fit patients mount vigorous sympathetic vasoconstriction, sustaining systolic BP until ~30–40% volume loss (Class III). Hypotension is therefore a LATE sign, and clinicians should not be falsely reassured by a normal BP — tachycardia and a narrowing pulse pressure are the earlier warnings.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A trauma patient is in Class IV haemorrhagic shock. Which management step is most appropriate?
options: Withhold blood products and give 2 L of crystalloid first
Delay tranexamic acid until 6 hours have passed
Activate the major haemorrhage protocol with balanced blood product resuscitation and urgent haemorrhage control
Aim for a supranormal systolic BP before controlling the source
Reassess in 30 minutes as the picture is likely to improve spontaneously
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Activate the major haemorrhage protocol with balanced blood product resuscitation and urgent haemorrhage control
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Class IV (>40%, >2000 mL) is immediately life-threatening. Management is to activate the major haemorrhage protocol, give balanced blood products (not large-volume crystalloid), obtain large-bore IV access, give tranexamic acid within 3 hours, use permissive hypotension until bleeding is controlled, and urgently stop the source. Delaying blood or TXA, or targeting a high BP before source control, worsens outcomes.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 70-year-old man is admitted with a BMI of 17 kg/m² and reports unplanned weight loss of 8% over the past 4 months. He is eating normally. What is his MUST score and risk category?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Score 3, high risk
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: BMI <18.5 scores 2, weight loss 5-10% scores 1, and there is no acute disease effect (he is eating). Total = 3, which is ≥2 and therefore high risk - refer to dietitian and treat.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which set of biochemical abnormalities is characteristic of refeeding syndrome?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Reintroduction of feeding drives a shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, producing hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, alongside thiamine deficiency. Thiamine should be given before feeding and electrolytes replaced with monitoring.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient screens with a total MUST score of 1. According to standard MUST guidance, what is the appropriate action?
options: Refer urgently to the nutrition support team
No further action needed for one year
Observe: document dietary intake for 3 days and repeat screening
Start NG feeding at full rate
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Observe: document dietary intake for 3 days and repeat screening
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: A score of 1 is medium risk. The recommended action is to observe, document food/fluid intake for 3 days, and repeat screening - escalating only if intake is inadequate. Active treatment (dietitian referral, nutrition support) is reserved for high risk (≥2).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A bedbound patient has a Braden scale score of 8. How should this be interpreted?
options: Very high risk of pressure ulcers
The patient already has a category 4 ulcer
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Very high risk of pressure ulcers
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The Braden scale runs the opposite way to Waterlow: a LOWER score means HIGHER risk. A score of ≤9 indicates very high risk, so a Braden of 8 warrants full preventive measures (SSKIN bundle).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient scores 17 on the Waterlow score. What risk category is this?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: High risk
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Waterlow runs so that higher = higher risk: ≥10 at risk, ≥15 high risk, ≥20 very high risk. A score of 17 falls in the high-risk band (≥15).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A sacral pressure ulcer shows full-thickness skin loss with visible subcutaneous fat but no exposed muscle, tendon, or bone. What EPUAP/NPUAP category is this?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Category 3
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Category 3 is full-thickness skin loss with subcutaneous fat visible but no exposed muscle, tendon, or bone. Exposed muscle/tendon/bone would make it category 4; a blister or partial-thickness loss would be category 2.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A trauma patient opens his eyes to a painful stimulus, uses inappropriate words, and localises to pain. What is his GCS?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Eyes open to pain = E2. Inappropriate words = V3. Localises to pain = M5. Total = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10, a moderate impairment. Always report the breakdown (E2V3M5), not just the total.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient's GCS falls from 14 to 8 over 20 minutes following a head injury. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Urgent senior review, secure the airway (anaesthetic support / consider intubation) and arrange urgent CT head
Give oral analgesia and repeat GCS in 4 hours
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Urgent senior review, secure the airway (anaesthetic support / consider intubation) and arrange urgent CT head
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: A drop of ≥2 points is significant deterioration, and GCS ≤8 means the airway is at risk ('GCS 8, intubate'). This mandates urgent airway support and CT head to identify an evolving intracranial cause.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which statement about the GCS is correct?
options: The verbal score has the greatest prognostic value
A total score alone is sufficient and the breakdown need not be documented
The motor component is the most prognostically important and the breakdown (E, V, M) should always be recorded
Intoxication has no effect on the score
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: The motor component is the most prognostically important and the breakdown (E, V, M) should always be recorded
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Motor response carries the greatest prognostic weight. The maximum score is 15, confounders such as intoxication, sedation and dysphasia can falsely lower it, and E, V and M must always be documented separately.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four components of the Apfel score for predicting PONV?
options: Duration of surgery over two hours
History of PONV or motion sickness
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Duration of surgery over two hours
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The simplified Apfel score uses exactly four factors, each worth 1 point: female sex, non-smoker, prior PONV/motion sickness, and anticipated post-operative opioid use. Duration of surgery is a recognised risk factor for PONV but is not part of the Apfel score.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient scores 3 on the Apfel score. What is the approximate predicted risk of PONV?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Apfel scores of 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 correspond to predicted PONV risks of approximately 10%, 20%, 40%, 60% and 80% respectively. A score of 3 therefore predicts about a 60% risk, warranting combination prophylaxis and modification of anaesthetic technique.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: For a high-risk patient, which prophylaxis approach is most appropriate?
options: Repeated doses of a single 5-HT₃ antagonist
Combination antiemetics from different receptor classes plus baseline risk reduction
A single dose of ondansetron only
Withholding all antiemetics until symptoms occur
High-dose volatile anaesthesia to ensure depth
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Combination antiemetics from different receptor classes plus baseline risk reduction
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Higher Apfel scores call for multimodal prophylaxis: combining agents that act on different receptors (e.g. ondansetron + dexamethasone ± a dopamine antagonist) is more effective than repeating one class. This is paired with baseline risk reduction such as propofol TIVA, avoiding volatiles/nitrous oxide and minimising opioids.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 58-year-old is booked for elective surgery. He has COPD requiring home oxygen and a BMI of 44. He is a current smoker with well-controlled hypertension. What is his ASA grade?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: ASA III
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: COPD on home oxygen and a BMI ≥40 (morbid obesity) represent severe systemic disease with substantive functional limitation, placing him at ASA III. Well-controlled hypertension and smoking alone would only reach ASA II, but the more severe features dictate the higher grade.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which patient is best classified as ASA IV?
options: A patient with septic shock requiring vasopressors
A pregnant woman with an uncomplicated pregnancy
A patient who had a myocardial infarction 8 months ago and is now asymptomatic
A brain-dead patient undergoing organ retrieval
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: A patient with septic shock requiring vasopressors
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: ASA IV is severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life — sepsis/DIC, recent (<3-month) MI/CVA/stent, or ESRD not on dialysis. Septic shock fits this. A healthy 30-year-old is ASA I, uncomplicated pregnancy is ASA II, an MI >3 months ago (now stable) is ASA III, and the brain-dead donor is ASA VI.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which statement about the ASA classification is correct?
options: It incorporates the type and complexity of the planned surgery
The 'E' suffix denotes an elective procedure
It grades the patient's baseline physical status and is a subjective clinical judgement
ASA V describes a declared brain-dead organ donor
A higher ASA grade is a precise, standalone predictor of individual mortality
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: It grades the patient's baseline physical status and is a subjective clinical judgement
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: ASA grades baseline patient fitness only and is inherently subjective. It does NOT incorporate the surgery type or airway difficulty in isolation. The 'E' suffix denotes emergency (not elective) surgery. ASA V is a moribund patient; VI is the brain-dead donor. ASA correlates with but does not solely determine mortality — it should be combined with surgical risk, functional capacity and frailty.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient with moderate cancer pain is inadequately controlled on regular paracetamol. According to the WHO analgesic ladder, what is the most appropriate next step?
options: Switch paracetamol to an NSAID only
Add a weak opioid such as codeine to the paracetamol
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Add a weak opioid such as codeine to the paracetamol
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Moving from step 1 to step 2 means adding a weak opioid (codeine, dihydrocodeine or tramadol) to the existing non-opioid — the non-opioid is continued, not replaced. Jumping straight to a strong opioid (step 3) is not indicated when the step-2 option has not been tried, and adjuvants are added on top rather than substituted for baseline analgesia.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient on regular morphine develops pinpoint pupils, drowsiness and a respiratory rate of 6/min. What is the immediate management?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Give naloxone
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The triad of pinpoint pupils, reduced consciousness and respiratory depression is opioid toxicity. Naloxone is the specific antagonist and is titrated (to respiratory rate, not full alertness, in palliative/dependent patients). Laxatives and antiemetics manage other opioid effects but do not treat life-threatening respiratory depression.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient with chronic pain and stage 4 chronic kidney disease requires a strong opioid. Which agent should be avoided?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Morphine
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Morphine's active metabolites (e.g. morphine-6-glucuronide) are renally cleared and accumulate in renal impairment, causing sedation, myoclonus and respiratory depression. Oxycodone, alfentanil, buprenorphine and fentanyl are preferred in significant renal impairment.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 68-year-old with AKI has a serum potassium of 7.1 mmol/L with peaked T waves on ECG. He has received calcium gluconate, insulin-dextrose and nebulised salbutamol but the potassium remains 6.9 mmol/L with persisting ECG changes. Which AEIOU indication does this represent?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: E — Electrolytes
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Refractory hyperkalaemia (K⁺ >6.5, or with ECG changes, not responding to medical management) is the 'E' indication for emergency RRT. Medical measures — calcium gluconate to protect the myocardium, insulin-dextrose and salbutamol to shift potassium — have failed, so dialysis is indicated.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which of the following poisonings is an established indication for haemodialysis (the 'I' in AEIOU)?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Methanol poisoning
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Methanol is one of the toxic alcohols ('A' in the BLAST mnemonic: Barbiturates, Lithium, Alcohols, Salicylates, Theophylline) that are dialysable. Paracetamol, warfarin, benzodiazepines and opioids have specific antidotes or supportive management and are not standard dialysis indications.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient with AKI develops a pericardial friction rub and confusion with a markedly elevated urea. What does AEIOU indicate?
options: Continue conservative management as this will resolve spontaneously
This represents fluid overload requiring ultrafiltration alone
This is uraemia — an urgent indication for RRT
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: This is uraemia — an urgent indication for RRT
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Uraemic pericarditis (friction rub) and uraemic encephalopathy (confusion) are emergency 'U' indications for renal replacement therapy. They mandate urgent dialysis rather than continued conservative management, and are not treated by diuretics or antibiotics.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 64-year-old man completes the IPSS and scores a total of 22 on the seven symptom questions. Into which severity band does this fall?
options: Cannot be classified without the QoL score
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Severe
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The IPSS symptom bands are 0-7 mild, 8-19 moderate, and 20-35 severe. A total of 22 falls in the severe band. The separate QoL/bother question (0-6) is reported alongside but is not required to classify the symptom band.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which of the following IPSS symptoms is classified as a storage (irritative) rather than a voiding (obstructive) symptom?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Urgency
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Storage/irritative symptoms are frequency, urgency and nocturia. The others listed (weak stream, straining, intermittency, incomplete emptying) are voiding/obstructive symptoms. Distinguishing the predominant symptom group helps guide treatment choice.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A man with BPH is started on finasteride. Which statement about this drug is correct?
options: It shrinks the prostate over months and lowers PSA
It provides rapid symptom relief within days
It commonly causes first-dose postural hypotension
It is an anticholinergic used for storage symptoms
It should be avoided in men with large prostates
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: It shrinks the prostate over months and lowers PSA
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Finasteride is a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor that shrinks the prostate gradually over months and is most useful in larger glands. It roughly halves PSA, which must be accounted for when interpreting PSA. Rapid relief and first-dose hypotension are features of alpha-blockers like tamsulosin.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A contrast-enhanced CT shows a cystic renal lesion with multiple thin septa and minimal smooth septal thickening, but no measurable enhancement. What is the appropriate management?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Surveillance follow-up imaging
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: These non-enhancing features (multiple thin septa, minimal smooth thickening) with no enhancement define Bosniak IIF (~5–10% malignant). IIF lesions are followed with surveillance imaging and should not be discharged, but do not warrant immediate surgery.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which single feature most reliably distinguishes a Bosniak III lesion requiring surgery from a Bosniak IIF lesion requiring follow-up?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Measurable enhancement of walls/septa
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Enhancement is the critical discriminator. Non-enhancing complexity (septa, calcification, minimal thickening) is IIF; measurable enhancement of thick/irregular walls or septa defines category III (~50% malignant), which mandates surgical management.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A renal cyst has an enhancing soft-tissue nodule adjacent to but independent of its wall. What is the Bosniak category and approximate malignancy risk?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Category IV, ~90%+
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: An enhancing soft-tissue/solid component adjacent to but independent of the wall/septa defines Bosniak IV, with ~90%+ malignant risk. Management is surgical resection, and most renal cancers are clear cell RCC.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the six IMDC (Heng) prognostic risk factors for metastatic RCC?
options: Hypercalcaemia (corrected calcium > upper limit of normal)
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The six IMDC factors are performance status <80%, <1 year to systemic treatment, anaemia, hypercalcaemia, neutrophilia and thrombocytosis. LDH is a component of the older MSKCC (Motzer) criteria, not the IMDC model.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient with metastatic clear cell RCC has 2 IMDC risk factors. Which risk group and approximate median overall survival does this correspond to?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Intermediate risk; ~23 months
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: 1-2 factors defines the intermediate risk group, with a median overall survival of approximately 23 months. 0 factors is favourable (~43 months) and 3-6 factors is poor (~8 months).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: In which clinical scenario is the IMDC model correctly applied?
options: Deciding whether a localised RCC needs partial or radical nephrectomy
Screening for RCC in a patient with painless haematuria
Prognostication and selecting first-line systemic therapy in metastatic RCC
Grading the histological aggressiveness of a resected tumour
Monitoring response to chemotherapy in muscle-invasive bladder cancer
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Prognostication and selecting first-line systemic therapy in metastatic RCC
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The IMDC (Heng) model stratifies patients with metastatic RCC to predict survival and guide first-line systemic therapy (e.g. ipilimumab+nivolumab for intermediate/poor risk, or TKI-based regimens). It does not apply to localised disease, tumour grading or screening.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A man with severe BPH (IPSS 24) fails medical therapy and undergoes TURP. He becomes confused with a low serum sodium intra-operatively. What is the likely cause?
options: An anaphylactic reaction to the anaesthetic
TURP syndrome from absorption of glycine irrigation fluid
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: TURP syndrome from absorption of glycine irrigation fluid
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: TURP syndrome is dilutional hyponatraemia and fluid overload caused by systemic absorption of hypotonic (glycine) irrigation fluid during resection, producing confusion, visual disturbance and cardiovascular upset. It is the classic complication of TURP.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient graded ASA IV is listed for major surgery. Which management step is most appropriate?
options: Proceed with no additional planning as ASA does not affect management
Early senior anaesthetic review with preoperative optimisation and HDU/ITU planning
Downgrade to ASA II to simplify booking
Avoid anaesthetic review to save time
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Early senior anaesthetic review with preoperative optimisation and HDU/ITU planning
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: A high ASA grade (III+/IV) flags substantial perioperative risk and should trigger senior anaesthetic review, optimisation of comorbidities, and consideration of higher-care (HDU/ITU) booking and prehabilitation. ASA is read alongside surgical severity and functional capacity.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 72-year-old arrives in ED with sudden right arm and facial weakness and slurred speech. Before calculating a ROSIER score, what is the single most important test to perform?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Capillary blood glucose
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Hypoglycaemia is a classic stroke mimic that can reproduce focal neurological deficits. Glucose must be checked and corrected before relying on the ROSIER score. CT follows to exclude haemorrhage, but glucose is the immediate bedside step.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient scores +1 for asymmetric arm weakness and +1 for speech disturbance, but had a witnessed seizure at onset (−1). What is the ROSIER total and its interpretation?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: +1, stroke likely
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Points: +1 (arm) +1 (speech) −1 (seizure) = +1. A total > 0 means stroke is likely and the stroke pathway should be activated. Note that a low or negative score does not exclude stroke.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A confirmed ischaemic stroke patient has an NIHSS of 18. Which band and clinical significance does this represent?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Moderate–severe stroke (16–20)
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: An NIHSS of 18 falls in the 16–20 band (moderate–severe). NIHSS quantifies severity and, alongside imaging and time from onset, helps guide thrombolysis and thrombectomy decisions and ongoing monitoring.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient has one clinical attack (optic neuritis) with MRI showing a single lesion. Which combination of findings must be demonstrated to diagnose MS by the McDonald Criteria?
options: Both dissemination in space and dissemination in time
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Both dissemination in space and dissemination in time
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: A clinically isolated syndrome (1 attack, 1 lesion) requires both DIS and DIT to be shown — via MRI and/or CSF — before MS can be diagnosed.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which of the following can substitute for dissemination in time (DIT) under the 2017 McDonald Criteria revision?
options: A raised CSF white cell count
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: CSF-specific oligoclonal bands
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The 2017 revision allows CSF-specific oligoclonal bands (present in CSF but not serum) to substitute for DIT, reflecting intrathecal IgG synthesis.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which set correctly lists the four characteristic CNS locations used to establish dissemination in space?
options: Optic nerve, basal ganglia, cerebellum, medulla
Periventricular, optic nerve, thalamus, spinal cord
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Periventricular, (juxta)cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: DIS requires ≥1 T2 lesion in ≥2 of these four areas: periventricular, (juxta)cortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 62-year-old man has progressive limb weakness. Examination shows wasting and fasciculations in both arms and legs, brisk reflexes with upgoing plantars, plus tongue fasciculation and a brisk jaw jerk. Sensation is normal. Which El Escorial category best fits?
options: Diagnosis excluded — sensory testing needed first
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Clinically Definite ALS
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: He has combined UMN + LMN signs in bulbar, cervical and lumbosacral regions — that is ≥3 regions, meeting the threshold for Clinically Definite ALS. Normal sensation is consistent with MND.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: What is the key conceptual change introduced by the Awaji criteria compared with the revised El Escorial criteria?
options: They add sensory nerve conduction abnormalities as a diagnostic criterion
They give EMG evidence of LMN dysfunction equal weight to clinical LMN signs
They require MRI confirmation of cord atrophy for diagnosis
They lower the number of regions needed for 'Definite' from 3 to 2
They mandate a therapeutic trial of riluzole before diagnosis
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: They give EMG evidence of LMN dysfunction equal weight to clinical LMN signs
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Awaji allows EMG findings (fibrillations, fasciculation potentials, chronic neurogenic changes) to substitute for clinical LMN signs in a region, improving early and sensitive diagnosis. It does not add sensory criteria or change region thresholds.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which of the following, if present, should most strongly prompt you to reconsider the diagnosis of MND and actively exclude a mimic?
options: A clear sensory level with saddle anaesthesia and urinary retention
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: A clear sensory level with saddle anaesthesia and urinary retention
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: MND characteristically SPARES sensation and sphincters. A sensory level with saddle anaesthesia and retention points to a structural/compressive lesion (e.g. cervical or cord pathology) — a mimic that must be excluded. The other findings are compatible with MND.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 34-year-old presents with acute right-sided facial droop. He cannot raise his right eyebrow or wrinkle his forehead, and cannot fully close the right eye. Which statement is most accurate?
options: This is a lower motor neurone palsy consistent with Bell's palsy
Forehead involvement indicates a UMN lesion such as a stroke
The eye can be left unprotected as it will recover quickly
Corticosteroids are contraindicated in this presentation
Complete eye closure would be expected in a House-Brackmann Grade VI
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: This is a lower motor neurone palsy consistent with Bell's palsy
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Forehead involvement (inability to raise the brow) indicates an LMN lesion, as in Bell's palsy - the whole half of the face is affected. A UMN lesion spares the forehead. Incomplete eye closure mandates eye protection, and prednisolone within 72h is indicated.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: On the House-Brackmann scale, at which grade does eye closure first become incomplete?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Grade IV
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Grades II and III retain complete eye closure (with minimal effort, then with effort). Grade IV (moderately severe) is defined by obvious disfiguring weakness, asymmetry at rest and incomplete eye closure - the key threshold at which corneal protection becomes critical.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient with a facial palsy is noted to have vesicles in the external auditory canal and severe ear pain. What is the most appropriate addition to management?
options: No change - manage identically to idiopathic Bell's palsy
Urgent surgical facial nerve decompression as first line
Antivirals, as this suggests Ramsay Hunt syndrome (VZV)
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Antivirals, as this suggests Ramsay Hunt syndrome (VZV)
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Ear-canal vesicles and pain suggest Ramsay Hunt syndrome from varicella-zoster virus reactivation. Management adds antivirals to corticosteroids. Eye protection remains essential, and it typically carries a worse prognosis than idiopathic Bell's palsy.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient with a traumatic spinal injury has no motor function below the neurological level, but retains perianal pinprick sensation and deep anal pressure on PR examination. There is no voluntary anal contraction. What is the AIS grade?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: AIS B
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Sacral sensory sparing is present (perianal sensation and deep anal pressure preserved), so the injury is incomplete — not AIS A. There is no motor function below the level (no VAC, no motor sparing), so it is sensory incomplete = AIS B. C and D require preserved motor function below the level.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: An 78-year-old with cervical spondylosis falls forwards and hyperextends the neck. He has marked weakness in both hands and forearms but only mild lower-limb weakness. Which incomplete cord syndrome is this?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Central cord syndrome
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Central cord syndrome is the commonest incomplete syndrome, classically from a hyperextension injury in an elderly patient with pre-existing cervical spondylosis. The centrally located corticospinal fibres serving the upper limbs are affected preferentially, so the arms are weaker than the legs.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which statement about complete versus incomplete spinal cord injury classification is correct?
options: Preservation of any sacral sparing (S4–5 sensation, deep anal pressure, or voluntary anal contraction) defines an incomplete injury
The neurological level of injury alone determines completeness
AIS grade A means normal neurological function
High-dose steroids are routinely recommended to improve AIS grade
Neurogenic shock is defined by hypotension with tachycardia
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Preservation of any sacral sparing (S4–5 sensation, deep anal pressure, or voluntary anal contraction) defines an incomplete injury
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Sacral sparing is the pivotal finding separating incomplete (AIS B–D, better prognosis) from complete (AIS A) injury. AIS A is complete injury; AIS E is normal. Steroids are controversial and not routine. Neurogenic shock is hypotension WITH bradycardia (sympathetic disruption), not tachycardia.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 28-year-old obese woman presents with headache, pulsatile tinnitus and papilloedema. Fundoscopy confirms bilateral disc swelling; she has a bilateral sixth nerve palsy but no other focal signs. MRI brain is normal. Which further step is essential BEFORE confidently diagnosing IIH?
options: CT venography or MR venography to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: CT venography or MR venography to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Normal standard imaging is required, but cerebral venous sinus thrombosis can mimic IIH and must be actively excluded with venography before the diagnosis is made. The sixth nerve palsy is a false localising sign and does not exclude IIH.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: According to the modified Dandy criteria, what is the expected CSF finding in IIH?
options: Raised opening pressure with high protein and low glucose
Raised opening pressure (>25 cm CSF) with normal CSF composition
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Raised opening pressure (>25 cm CSF) with normal CSF composition
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: IIH requires a raised CSF opening pressure on lumbar puncture (>25 cm CSF / >250 mm) but with otherwise normal CSF constituents. Abnormal composition points to an alternative cause such as infection, inflammation or haemorrhage.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which of the following is the definitive, first-line management for idiopathic intracranial hypertension?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Weight loss
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Weight loss is the definitive first-line treatment and can be curative. Acetazolamide reduces CSF production as pharmacological support; surgery (optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunt) is reserved for threatened vision. Steroids and oral contraceptives can actually precipitate IIH.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A cerebral AVM has a nidus of 4 cm, lies adjacent to the internal capsule, and drains via deep veins. What is its Spetzler-Martin grade?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Grade IV
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Size 3-6 cm = 2 points; internal capsule is eloquent = 1 point; deep venous drainage = 1 point. Total 4 = Grade IV, indicating high surgical morbidity.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which of the following contributes 1 point (eloquent location) in the Spetzler-Martin grading system?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Brainstem
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Eloquent areas include sensorimotor, language and visual cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus, internal capsule, brainstem, cerebellar peduncles and deep cerebellar nuclei. The brainstem qualifies; the other listed sites are considered non-eloquent.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: What does the Spetzler-Martin grade primarily predict?
options: Likelihood of seizure control after treatment
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Risk/morbidity of surgical resection
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The scale estimates operative risk to guide whether an AVM is a good surgical candidate. It does not estimate rupture risk (roughly 2-4%/year independently) and does not replace multidisciplinary judgement.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient has a suspected TIA that fully resolved. According to current NICE guidance, what is the correct management?
options: Calculate ABCD2 and only refer if it is 4 or more
Reassure and arrange a routine outpatient appointment
No treatment as symptoms have resolved
Start warfarin immediately in all cases
Aspirin 300 mg immediately and specialist assessment within 24 hours
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Aspirin 300 mg immediately and specialist assessment within 24 hours
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: NICE (2019) treats all suspected TIA as high-risk and no longer uses ABCD2 to triage. Give aspirin 300 mg immediately (unless contraindicated) and refer for specialist assessment within 24 hours; if the patient is on an anticoagulant, exclude haemorrhage with imaging first.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which statement about the ABCD2 score is correct for UK finals?
options: A low ABCD2 safely allows routine (non-urgent) referral
NICE no longer recommends it to risk-stratify TIA; all suspected TIA is treated as high-risk
It is used to decide thrombolysis in acute stroke
It includes cholesterol and smoking as components
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: NICE no longer recommends it to risk-stratify TIA; all suspected TIA is treated as high-risk
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: ABCD2 (Age, BP, Clinical features, Duration, Diabetes) once triaged TIA by 2-day stroke risk, but NICE (2019) abandoned it as a gatekeeper: every suspected TIA gets aspirin 300 mg and specialist review within 24 hours. It plays no role in thrombolysis decisions.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 5-year-old refuses to weight-bear on the right leg. Temperature is 39.0°C, ESR is 55 mm/hr and WCC is 15 × 10⁹/L. How many Kocher predictors are present and what is the approximate probability of septic arthritis?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: 4 predictors, ~99%
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: All four predictors are positive: non-weight-bearing, fever > 38.5°C (39.0°C), ESR > 40 (55), and WCC > 12 (15). A score of 4 corresponds to roughly a 99% probability of septic arthritis, mandating urgent surgical washout and IV antibiotics.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which of the following is the definitive investigation to confirm septic arthritis of the hip?
options: Joint aspiration for Gram stain, culture and synovial WCC
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Joint aspiration for Gram stain, culture and synovial WCC
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Bloods and ultrasound support the diagnosis (an effusion on USS, raised inflammatory markers), but joint aspiration is definitive — frank pus or organisms on Gram stain/culture confirm septic arthritis. X-rays are often normal early.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A child has a Kocher score of 0 but the clinician remains concerned about septic arthritis on examination. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Discharge with safety-netting as septic arthritis is excluded
Do not rely on the score alone; proceed to further assessment and consider joint aspiration
Reassure and treat as transient synovitis without further tests
Start oral antibiotics and review in one week
Arrange an outpatient MRI in two weeks
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Do not rely on the score alone; proceed to further assessment and consider joint aspiration
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: A low Kocher score does not fully exclude septic arthritis when clinical suspicion is high. Because delayed treatment causes irreversible joint destruction and AVN, clinical judgement should override a reassuring score, warranting urgent orthopaedic assessment and aspiration.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 24-year-old woman is assessed for joint pain. She can dorsiflex both little fingers beyond 90°, oppose both thumbs to her forearms, hyperextend both elbows beyond 10°, but cannot hyperextend her knees or place her palms flat on the floor. What is her Beighton score?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Little fingers (2) + thumbs (2) + elbows (2) = 6. Knees and palms-to-floor score 0. In an adult, ≥5 suggests generalised joint hypermobility, so this is positive.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which statement about the Beighton score is most accurate?
options: It is a screening tool for generalised joint hypermobility, not a diagnosis in itself
A score ≥5 in an adult diagnoses hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
Palms-to-floor scores one point per side
It reliably excludes vascular EDS and Marfan syndrome
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: It is a screening tool for generalised joint hypermobility, not a diagnosis in itself
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The Beighton score (max 9) screens for generalised hypermobility. hEDS requires the full 2017 criteria. Palms-to-floor is a single midline point. A high score neither diagnoses hEDS nor excludes serious disorders like vascular EDS or Marfan syndrome.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A hypermobile patient reports translucent thin skin, easy bruising, and a family history of a relative who died suddenly from a ruptured artery. What is the most important next step?
options: Reassure — hypermobility is benign and requires no action
Refer for specialist genetics/cardiology assessment to evaluate for vascular EDS
Repeat the Beighton score in 12 months
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Refer for specialist genetics/cardiology assessment to evaluate for vascular EDS
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Thin translucent skin, easy bruising and a family history of arterial rupture raise concern for vascular EDS (COL3A1), which carries a risk of arterial and organ rupture. This mandates specialist genetics and cardiology assessment rather than reassurance or conservative measures alone.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 24-year-old man with no family history of Marfan syndrome has an aortic root Z-score of 2.4 on echocardiography and bilateral ectopia lentis on slit-lamp examination. Under the revised Ghent criteria, what is the correct conclusion?
options: Genetic testing for FBN1 is mandatory before any diagnosis can be made
A systemic score ≥7 is additionally required
This meets criteria only for MASS phenotype
Ectopia lentis syndrome should be diagnosed instead
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Marfan syndrome is confirmed
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The two cardinal features — aortic root dilatation (Z-score ≥2) and ectopia lentis — together confirm Marfan syndrome even without family history, FBN1 testing, or a systemic score. This is the highest-weighted combination in Ghent-2.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which single systemic feature is worth the most points (3) in the Ghent-2 systemic score for Marfan syndrome?
options: Wrist sign and thumb sign present together
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Wrist sign and thumb sign present together
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Wrist AND thumb sign together score 3 points (either sign alone scores 1). Pectus carinatum, dural ectasia, protrusio acetabuli and pneumothorax each score 2; facial features score 1. A total ≥7 is contributory.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A patient being assessed for Marfan syndrome is found to have DOWNWARD dislocation of the lenses and a history of venous thrombosis. Which action is most important?
options: Immediately proceed to prophylactic aortic root replacement
Reassure and discharge, as this excludes connective-tissue disease
Test for homocystinuria, an important mimic
Apply Ghent criteria and diagnose Marfan on the ectopia lentis alone
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Test for homocystinuria, an important mimic
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: Homocystinuria classically causes DOWNWARD lens dislocation plus thromboembolism and must be excluded before diagnosing Marfan (where lens dislocation is typically upward). Ectopia lentis alone does not confirm Marfan, and testing for the mimic takes priority.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 30-year-old inverts his ankle playing football. He has pain in the malleolar zone. On examination there is no bony tenderness over either malleolus, and he was able to walk 4 steps immediately after the injury and again in the department. Which is the most appropriate action?
options: No X-ray is required — the Ottawa Ankle Rules are negative
Request ankle and foot X-rays as pain is present
Request an ankle X-ray but not a foot X-ray
Admit for observation and repeat examination in 24 hours
Request MRI to exclude occult fracture
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: No X-ray is required — the Ottawa Ankle Rules are negative
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: An ankle X-ray is only indicated with malleolar-zone pain PLUS malleolar bony tenderness OR inability to weight-bear (4 steps, immediately and in the ED). With no bony tenderness and preserved weight-bearing, the rule is negative and its near-100% sensitivity means fracture is effectively excluded, so imaging can be safely withheld.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the Ottawa Knee Rule criteria for requesting a knee X-ray?
options: A visible knee effusion on inspection
Tenderness at the head of the fibula
Inability to flex the knee to 90°
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: A visible knee effusion on inspection
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The five Ottawa Knee Rule criteria are: age ≥55, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular-head tenderness, inability to flex to 90°, and inability to weight-bear (4 steps both immediately and in the ED). A visible effusion is not part of the rule.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which statement best describes the diagnostic performance of the Ottawa Rules?
options: High specificity, so a positive rule confirms a fracture
They are equally sensitive and specific and confirm fractures
Low sensitivity, so they miss most significant fractures
They replace the need for any clinical judgement
High sensitivity, so a negative rule safely excludes a clinically significant fracture
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: High sensitivity, so a negative rule safely excludes a clinically significant fracture
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The rules are highly sensitive (approaching 100%) but have low specificity. This makes them an excellent rule-OUT tool: a negative rule reliably excludes clinically significant fracture and allows imaging to be avoided. A positive rule only identifies who needs an X-ray — it does not confirm a fracture is present.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: A 22-year-old man sustains a closed femoral shaft fracture in a road traffic collision. Around 48 hours later he becomes confused and breathless, with an SpO2 of 88% on air and a petechial rash over his upper chest and conjunctivae. Which diagnostic criteria best support the likely diagnosis?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Gurd and Wilson criteria
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The picture (young patient, femoral fracture, deterioration at 24-72h with hypoxia, confusion and petechiae) is classic fat embolism syndrome, diagnosed clinically using Gurd and Wilson's criteria (1 major + 4 minor).

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: Which of the following is a MAJOR criterion in Gurd's criteria for fat embolism syndrome?
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Petechial rash
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.explanation: The major criteria are respiratory insufficiency, cerebral involvement, and petechial rash. Tachycardia, pyrexia, raised ESR and thrombocytopenia are all minor criteria.

investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.question: What is the mainstay of treatment for fat embolism syndrome?
options: Supportive care with oxygen/ventilatory support and ICU management
investigations__RISK SCORES & CRITERIA__.answer: Supportive care with oxygen/ventilatory support and ICU management
